author: Bukola Oladunjoye
title: Living and Losing the ECOWAS Dream: Borders, Belonging, and Betrayal
content:
As I entered Benin, I waited for the air to change. I stood at that threshold with the quiet anticipation of someone expecting a revelation, for the people to look far apart from me, for some element of differentiation, something to confirm I was no longer in Nigeria. I was searching, almost desperately, for the feeling of foreignness. Instead, what greeted me was the mandatory walk on foot across a stretch of dusty no-man’s-land, the heat sitting on my shoulders like a familiar relative. There was the service charge for entry, slipped across a counter with the practiced nonchalance of a transaction that exists in no official ledger. And there were the sweaty hands that stamped my passport, unhurried, unbothered, as though the act of dividing one people from another was simply another Tuesday. Beyond that, not much. Only the invisible lines drawn by chubby hands across a colonial round table, lines that speak more to the boundaries of colonial reach than to any real difference in identity or people. The same okadas weaved through traffic on both sides. The same smell of fried plantain hung in the air. The same sun.


Benin


My first thought: why is there no train across this coast? A coast declared a unified body by ECOWAS long before Europe had anything resembling the Schengen region. A single rail line from Lagos to Accra, threading through Cotonou and Lomé, would do more for West African integration than a thousand protocols signed in air-conditioned conference rooms. The European Union did not become real to its people through treaties, it became real the moment a German student could board a train in Berlin and wake up in Paris without once showing a passport. We have the treaties. We have the protocols. We have been a free movement zone, on paper, since 1979. What we do not have is the infrastructure that turns a political agreement into a lived experience. Instead, we walk. We sweat. We pay.


My first real differentiation came through language. The local I approached spoke differently, but even that gap traced back to an interrupted history. His was a colonial tongue, French shaped by Beninese breath and rhythm, as much as the English I rushed to speak in return, hoping he would understand: ‘I’d like to book a ride to Ouidah.’ He looked at me with the patient amusement of someone who had translated themselves their entire life, and we found each other somewhere in the middle, two Africans borrowing the languages of our respective colonisers to speak to one another on African soil. There is something quietly absurd about that, and something quietly devastating. We were not foreign to each other. Only our inherited tongues were.


We stopped in Ouidah for a day and a half, and the city unfolded like a quiet invitation, an adventure of discovery that immediately planted the intention to return. There is a particular kind of place that refuses to be consumed in a single visit, that withholds just enough of itself to ensure you come back. Ouidah is that place. The best trips end on an unfinished note, like cutlery rested neatly across a plate, signalling: I am not done tasting this.


Ouidah


But Ouidah was painful to explore. Not the loud, declarative pain of a wound freshly opened, but the dull, persistent ache of something that has never properly healed. I could not stop my mind from wandering, what would this city’s reality look like without the colonial interruption? What identity would it have assumed, what architecture, what cuisine, what music, without the chaos of its exploitation? The Python Temple – a local devotional site hosting live snakes – still stands, its sacred serpents moving slowly across the cool floor, carrying in their bodies a spirituality that survived everything. The Zomachi market still hums. But underneath it all, Ouidah carries the weight of what was taken from it.


Standing at the Door of No Return, I felt the ground shift slightly beneath me, not physically, but in the way that certain places demand a recalibration of the self. The monument stands at the edge of the Atlantic, facing the ocean that swallowed so many. The same ocean that connects Lagos to the Americas, that carried away millions and brought back almost nothing. A line from a Christmas carol I had sung thoughtlessly for years suddenly split open with new meaning: for slave is our brother. I had sung it as a child in church, in the rote way of someone reciting words without weight. Standing there, the words gained …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Sudan Nashra: Military strikes RSF convoy inside Chadian territory, sparks regional concerns | Kauda fighting pushes Otoro groups to demand Hilu’s removal from SPLM-N leadership | US proposes nationwide arms embargo on Sudan in Security Council
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

here

.


Washington is pushing in the United Nations Security Council to take the Darfur arms embargo nationwide.


US Senior Advisor on Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos put the proposal on the table on Monday, after first floating the idea at a council session in June. The draft would expand the 2005 Darfur sanctions regime to all of Sudan, while explicitly bringing drones and related technology under the embargo. The current regime expires in September unless amended or renewed.


Boulos pointed to the growing toll from drone warfare, saying drones accounted for nearly 80 percent of casualties this year and that both sides continue to strike civilians and civilian infrastructure.


Khartoum rejected the proposal outright. Sudan’s ambassador to the UN Al-Harith Idriss said applying the same restrictions nationwide would amount to equating “the state institutions and the rebel militia,” calling the proposal an attack on Sudan’s sovereignty.


Washington has to get past Russia and China, which both pushed back against expanding the sanctions regime and can veto any council resolution. So while the proposal has support from some council members, it is unlikely to go anywhere without a compromise.


Sudan’s drone war crossed its borders twice over the past days.


In western Sudan, military drones struck a convoy of hundreds of Rapid Support Forces vehicles on August 20 inside Chad’s eastern Ennedi region, near the Sudanese border. Two Sudanese military sources said the convoy had been assembled over several weeks at camps in southeastern Libya, and was preparing to enter Darfur through Chad using a new route through North Darfur’s Wadi Howar.


Chad condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty and warned that it reserved the right to respond, prompting the African Union to call for restraint and dialogue to prevent a regional escalation. The Sudanese military has yet to comment. 


On the other side of the country, the military said a strategic drone crossed into Blue Nile State from Ethiopian territory and was shot down over Dindro. 


Inside the RSF camp, its main ally in the war and its parallel government, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, continues to grapple with an internal crisis that is becoming harder to contain.


Fighting with one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, has returned to Kauda, the movement’s political and military center in South Kordofan, with control shifting between the two sides over the past two weeks.


RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo intervened and called for a ceasefire, but overlapping control on the ground made that impossible to sustain. The ceasefire collapsed, and Otoro fighters regained the upper hand in Kauda.


Some Otoro groups are now calling for Hilu to step down and are seeking alliances with other Nuba Mountains constituencies to challenge a political order that the SPLM-N has dominated for decades, but which has increasingly been concentrated in a narrow circle around Hilu, two Otoro leaders told Mada Masr.


And while there is still no end in sight to the war’s battles, Khartoum is preparing to use September’s UN General Assembly in New York to consolidate a post-Khartoum political posture and present its vision for Sudan’s political and institutional order after the war, according to Sudanese diplomatic and government sources informed of the preparations. 


Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan remains the leading option to head the delegation. But US sanctions imposed on him in 2025 could make his participation complicated, prompting the government to consider other senior officials if necessary.


The government plans to put its internal political dialogue on the New York agenda. The process, now being hurried in Khartoum, is to be presented as nationally owned, with international actors there to support and facilitate rather than dictate its agenda or outcome.


But a political source close to the dialogue said New York will test the international response to a process whose current, state-curated form is already being rejected by parts of the civilian political camp. 


Sudanese political and civilian forces, opposed to both the war and a military-led political process, rejected Burhan’s call for a dialogue, saying that any process launched while fighting continues — and conducted under military control — would reproduce …

author: WoMin
title: On Language and the Pedagogy of Liberation
content:
Across Africa, colonialism was not only a project of economic exploitation and political domination; it was also a project of language and cultural control. Colonial rule sought to determine not only who governed and who had access to resources but also elevated European languages as symbols of intelligence and authority, while African languages were systematically marginalised. 


African literature captured this contradiction. In

So Long a Letter

, Mariama Bâ writes from within the tensions of expressing African women’s realities through a language inherited from colonial rule. Ama Ata Aidoo’s novel

Our Sister Killjoy

, similarly, exposes the uneasy relationship between English as a language of literary expression and also as a reminder of cultural displacement. These reflections continue to resonate with present-day realities across the continent, where language remains deeply entangled with questions of power, culture, identity, class, gender, and belonging.  


Today, access to education, legal systems, government services, and political participation in many African countries still depends heavily on competence in colonial languages such as English, French, or Portuguese.  


In Nigeria, for example, although more than 250 languages are spoken across the country, English remains the dominant language of governance, education or even policy discourse. Similar dynamics persist elsewhere on the continent. In Tanzania, although Kiswahili is the national language, many court judgments continue to be delivered in English. Citizens who do not understand English must depend on interpreters to comprehend legal decisions affecting their lives. 


For peasant and working-class women confronting mining, oil extraction, logging, large-scale agricultural investments, and other extractive projects, language exclusions carry profound consequences especially for rural women whose language is deeply tied to their relationship to land, water, forests, food systems, ancestry, and survival.  


Where information about government-proposed projects is often delivered in foreign languages without clarifying their implications including the terms of the proposed project, the risks it poses, the compensation being offered, or the legal mechanisms available to challenge it, their ability to give meaningful consent or organise resistance against it, then language becomes a question of power. 


Language in Women Learning Liberation and Translation as a Tool of Resistance

 


Language was central to the development of

Women Learning Liberation

  (WLL), WoMin’s 18-month political education course for frontline women activists. The first WLL cohort began in July 2024, bringing together 60 women from Cameroon, Guinea Conakry, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, South Africa, and Uganda. From the beginning, WLL understood political education not as the transfer of knowledge from experts to communities, but as a process of collective learning rooted in women’s own experiences and struggles. 


The Ugandan WLL cohort spoke eight languages and represented five different community struggles. English could provide a common language for some discussions, but relying exclusively on it would have risked excluding women from fully expressing their experiences, questions, analysis, and political imagination. WLL therefore deliberately incorporated interpretation into the political education process. Facilitation moved between English, Luganda, Runyoro, and Kinyarwanda, while participants themselves became active in ensuring that interpretation was taking place. 


As

Ugandan facilitator Sostine Namanya

 explained: “Language can work, but language needs to be budgeted for, language needs to be prepped for.” 


In many African contexts, people come from diverse language backgrounds and often speak multiple languages. While English or French may serve as common languages, reliance on colonial languages can reproduce unequal power relations and weaken movements. Interpretation and translation therefore become powerful tools for building multilingual and robust movements capable of deepening collective participation.  


In 2024, WoMin launched materials supporting the

Right To Say NO  campaign in East Africa

 in five languages, which join a plethora of knowledge materials and resources such as its award-winning film,

Women Hold up the Sky

 (2021) and a comic book,

Voices against Extractivism: Sheroes for Change

. The act of interpretation and …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies: A Community of Practice to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence
content:
Over the past year, Liberation Alliance Africa has sustained the

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Indigenous Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

. This Community of Practice is a collective of African feminist scholars, practitioners, organisers, artists, and movement builders committed to the dreaming and making of a world free from sexual violence through knowledge bridges.


Sexual violence continues to impact communities across the African continent, and class, ethnicity and religion play a critical role in making civilians in conflict-affected countries particularly more vulnerable. It disproportionately affects women and girls, and ethnic, gender and racialized minorities. Sexual violence is compounded by conflict, displacement, poverty, and gender inequality. It remains significantly under-reported due to stigma and under-prosecuted? Due to weak and corrupt justice systems. Sexual violence includes rape and sexual assault, sexual coercion and exploitation, including trafficking for sexual exploitation and conflict-related sexual violence such as using rape as a weapon of war. It affects people of any gender and age. 


Our starting premise is simple: sexual violence on the continent cannot be understood, let alone addressed, through frameworks that treat colonialism as history rather than a structural force that continues to shape theory, practice, and response to sexual violence. 


Coloniality was

coined

by Peruvian philosopher and sociologist Aníbal Quijano, and it describes the long-lasting pattern of power produced by colonial rule and shape

s

 how we approach epistemological frameworks through which violence is understood.

Epistemology deals with questions concerning the nature, scope, and sources of knowledge.

 A meaningful analysis of sexual violence must begin by seeking to decolonise knowledge and epistemic structures. This analysis requires us to interrogate the assumptions that underpin dominant theories, question whose expertise is legitimised, and create space for African feminist epistemologies to shape how violence is understood, prevented, and responded to. 


We felt an urgent need to organise as scholars and practitioners to generate new frameworks grounded in our histories, political realities, and lived experiences. Our analyses are rooted in our confrontation of the neo-colonial state, the global imperialist, extractive and patriarchal systems that shape our everyday existence. We arrive as feminists in service of a liberatory project, convinced that knowledge-making is itself a site of feminist struggle. 


As the CoP came together through both intentional convening and organic growth, we began organising our work around three enquiries that we believe are critical to envisioning a decolonial feminist approach to preventing and responding to sexual violence in Africa. 


The first enquiry,

Whose Knowledge? An Audit of the Current Knowledge Systems within Sexual Violence Prevention and Response in Africa

 examines the dominant literature, asks whose voices have shaped the field, whose knowledge has been marginalised, and what becomes possible when African feminist scholarship is placed at the centre of analysis. 


The second enquiry,

 The Coloniality of Sexual Violence: Gender, Power, Sovereignty, and the Neo-Colonial State,

 advances interventions on sexual violence that explicitly interrogate the role and impact of hetero-patriarchal colonial racial-capitalism, alongside the complicity of neo-colonial states, in producing and sustaining conditions of gendered violence. 


The third enquiry,

Truth-telling and Epistemic Sovereignty in the Prevention and Response Continuum

, centres on indigenous and endogenous knowledge systems as essential practice-based frameworks for reimagining prevention, response, healing, accountability, and collective safety.


The Imperative of Recentering African Epistemologies


At Liberation Alliance Africa, we believe African women and gender-expansive people’s knowledge-making and world-building are crucial to de-westernising normative assumptions and dominant approaches. African women and gender-expansive scholars must nurture new ways of knowing and being- knowledge that doesn’t just challenge dominant views, but creates a rich foundation for how we understand reality and tackle life’s critical questions.


For a long time, African women and gender minorities were treated as …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Marikana’s wounds still bleed 14 years after police massacre
content:
Fourteen years after police opened fire on striking mineworkers at Marikana, the massacre is remembered not only for the 34 men who were killed, but for their absence in the lives of their families.


For some, the memory is of a father who never came home. For others, it is the loss of a breadwinner, a brother or a son. And for those who were children when the killings happened, it is the experience of growing up with memories that have become increasingly distant, while the questions about justice remain.


At a commemoration marking 14 years since the massacre, the families, activists and academics reflected on what Marikana means more than a decade later – and on its place in South Africa’s longer history of protest, police violence and struggles for dignity.


For the Socio-Economic Rights Institute of South Africa (Seri), which has represented the families since 2012, the central question remains accountability. Seri secured payments for 35 of the 37 families whose loved ones were killed by police. Two families have received no compensation.


Seri’s executive director, Nomzamo Zondo said the compensation process itself reflected a deeper problem in how the state understood the loss suffered by the families. “Part of that is a narrative that what the state is interested in compensating is the income that the miners would have earned. They do not want to account for the husbands, brothers, sons and fathers that they took away from the families,” she said.


For Zondo, compensation alone cannot address the significance of Marikana. The state also needs to acknowledge that the massacre should never have happened, she argued: “That’s what a public holiday on the 16

th

 of August would mean. It would say: we are saying never, never again.”


She said this was particularly important given the continued use of force by police in managing protests. “We’ve seen that police continue to manage protests through the use of violence. They have continuously refused to accept that their role is to facilitate protests as a constitutional right.”


Zondo also pointed to the failure to implement recommendations made by the panel of experts on public order policing and the management of protests. The panel completed its work in 2018, but its recommendations remain largely unimplemented.


Squalid living conditions in the informal settlement, Nkaneng, in the shadow of Marikana platinum mine, a source of immense wealth for the owners in 2012, Lonmin. Archive photo by The Benchmarks Foundation


Another major concern, she said, was the failure of the National Prosecuting Authority to bring those responsible for the 16 August killings to court. “Every year, of course, when the anniversary comes, there is an explanation that work is being done,” Zondo said. “But now we are like one year short from 15 years since the massacre. We are just 12 years since the Commission finalised its report and recommended that the NPA must investigate and charge whoever is responsible.”


The question, she said, was whether there was “really an intention to hold anyone accountable for the deaths of the 16

th

 of August”.


For the families, however, the consequences of Marikana are not measured only by the progress of criminal investigations or compensation claims. They are lived in the absence of loved ones.


‘I still have that memory’


NowilI Nungu was 15 when her father, Jackson Lehopa, was killed at Marikana. Today, at 29, she remembers him through the ordinary moments of their life together: travelling to school on a bicycle, buying him a Coke and watching him repair the bicycle whenever it broke.


“I have so many memories with my dad,” Nungu said. She was the only girl among six children and had been living with her father in Rustenburg while her mother moved back to the Eastern Cape.


By the time of the massacre, Nungu had moved to the Eastern Cape with her mother. The family did not have electricity and relied on the radio for news. Her father normally called every day after returning from the koppie to tell them he was safe. But that day, he did not call.


Crosses erected at the koppie as a symbol of lives lost on 16 August 2012. Archive photo by Muzi Mzoyi


Sebolai Liau lost his father, the late Janefeke Raphael Liau, at Marikana. For him, the question of justice remains unresolved. “I think regarding the Marikana massacre, there is no justice. I don’t think it will ever be served, but for now it has not been, and there are no signs …
sourceTags: Socio-Economic Rights Institute of South Africa (SERI)

author: Linda Ngari
title: Hybrid Repression: Coordinated Attacks on Rwanda Press Freedom
content:
The paradox of press freedom in Rwanda is that despite the advent of alternative media, younger journalists are more controlled than their older counterparts. “Today’s generation? Yeah, they’re getting more fear than we used to,” 47-year-old Rubens Mukunzi said in a phone interview. Rubens has experienced a Rwanda before Kagame’s 26-year presidency. He was 15 when the genocide that killed at least 800,000 Rwandans happened. The same year that 32-year-old Samuel Baker Byansi was born. While Rubens practised journalism in his home country for 13 years before he fled to America in 2013, Samuel practised for half the time, having started in 2016 and fleeing to Europe in 2022. Rubens had never been arrested for his work even though he earned the name “Mr Bean” from his comic commentary on Rwandan politics through his radio show at the time. But Samuel recalls being arrested more than four times for his work.


In a phone interview, Samuel narrates one of the arrests in 2022 that upended his plans to ask his girlfriend to marry him. “They arrested me for something not serious. I had tweeted that journalist

Kakwenza Rukirabashaija

 fled Uganda. I was detained for like four days. No communication. It disturbed me. I had my proposal that Saturday. I was arrested on Tuesday.” Samuel being arrested for a tweet is indicative of the government’s online surveillance to control free speech and limit the use of social media for political dissent.


Within three months of gathering this report, artist and YouTuber

Aimable Karasira

 was killed (May 6), and Rwandan authorities confirmed the arrest (May 1) of YouTubers Nsanzimana Augustin and Niyonshuti Emmanuel for “suspected spreading of false information” via their

YouTube channel

,

Imbarutso ya Demokarasi

 (The Rise of Democracy). Even though YouTubing is barely profitable in Rwanda since YouTube ads were

suspended

 in 2021. About 10 of the 13 imprisoned Rwandan journalists recorded on the Committee to Protect Journalists’

database

 are YouTubers, illustrating the paradox of press freedom in the country, where the rise of the internet and alternative media has ironically stirred up more repression.


As an early career journalist, Samuel underwent a compulsory civic education programme called

Itorero ry’Igihugu

. A report by Democracy in Africa explains that the programme was

introduced

 in 2009 as part of President Paul Kagame’s post-genocide ideology for the making of a “new Rwandan citizen”, known as

Umunyarwanda.

 Rubens, 30 at the time, was never a student of this programme. Samuel narrates his experience in his

book

 From

Watchdogs to Traitors: The less you know, the more you believe

. “The programme offers certificates symbolizing their support for the RPF. President Kagame holds the honorary title,

Intore Izirusha Intambwe

, a significant figure for all programme participants,” Samuel wrote. In the book, he recounts a time he was arrested for publishing a story titled “Eat and Die: Rwanda Supermarket Selling Toxic Meat”.


Samuel also mentions being offered US$500 by Rwandan authorities trying to recruit him as a government informant. “He [a police officer] expressed the desire to work closely with me in the interest of our country,” he wrote. The offer was backed by enticing dinners at high-end restaurants, free fuel at certain gas stations, tax exemptions, and a get-out-of-jail-free card for the times Samuel violated traffic rules.


 “In the beginning, of course, they don’t recruit you by telling you, ‘You are going to work for us,’ but they come as friends. ‘We want you to be friends with us. We have something to offer, which is a little bit better than what you earn.’  I remember when I bought my first car in Rwanda, and it was supposed to pay taxes of, like, five million Rwandan francs. And then one guy in the police intelligence called the revenue [Rwanda Revenue Authority] and told them, ‘Ah, this is our boy. You don’t need to tax him all this much.’ And just like that, I got my car without any tax paid. It’s like a psychological bribe somehow. So when the same person calls to ask for a favour of talking about someone online, you don’t have the capacity to say no. They give you all those privileges, and they give you this money, but in return you are compromising your own ethics, and this is what they want. But they also want you to maintain your credibility as a journalist, such that when you defend them, it becomes a little bit credible …

author: Gedeon Baleke
title: Africa’s Pension Funds Are Already Allowed to Invest at Home. They Don’t.
content:
Reformers keep asking governments to raise the ceilings on where domestic institutional capital can go. The ceilings are nowhere near being reached and one December in Ghana explains why. This article is published on 

African Arguments 

ahead of the

African Development Summit

 which takes place on 18 September 2026.


Nigeria’s pension regulator permits funds to hold up to 15 per cent of assets in private equity. Industry assets now stand above ₦31 trillion. Actual take-up sits far below the ceiling. Ghana’s regulator allows up to 25 per cent in private funds; actual allocations to alternatives stand at just 0.58 per cent.


In Nigeria, PenCom itself points to a supply-side constraint, a shortage of qualifying, investable funds yet the broader pattern across the continent suggests the deeper friction is not the availability of paper, but the appetite for it.


That is the fact that should reorganise the argument about domestic capital in Africa. The headroom exists. It goes unused. Whatever is stopping African savings from financing African production, it is not the rulebook. That means the reform most often demanded, a higher permitted allocation, would change almost nothing.


The ACD Summit on 18 September 2026 will debate major questions of domestic investment, development financing, and capital flight.


The question matters more this year than last. When the OECD released its preliminary figures in April, aid from the world’s wealthiest donors had fallen 23.1 per cent in 2025 to $174.3 billion. That was the steepest single-year contraction on record and the second consecutive annual decline. Bilateral aid to sub-Saharan Africa fell 26.3 per cent. In a subsequent June projections report, the OECD forecasts a further 11.6 per cent drop in bilateral aid to sub-Saharan Africa in 2026, with health financing potentially falling by as much as 63 per cent below its 2022 peak.


The reflex has been to point at remittances. Roughly $124 billion was sent home by Africans abroad in the same year, about twice what the continent received in official development assistance. It is the wrong comfort, and not only because the two flows are different sizes of the same thing. They do different work. Remittances are transfers between households. They pay school fees, clinic bills, rent and funeral costs, and they are extraordinarily good at that. They do not build a district hospital, capitalise a fertiliser plant, or underwrite a twenty-year power purchase agreement.


The pool that could do those things is institutional and already domestic. African pension funds and insurers hold around $775 billion in assets, according to the Africa Finance Corporation’s State of Africa’s Infrastructure Report 2025, of which $455 billion is in pensions and $320 billion in insurance. Add sovereign wealth funds and the African Development Bank’s Solomon Quaynor puts the figure at $2.1 trillion. The AFC’s 2025 report notes that in some countries, nearly 70 to 80 per cent of institutional portfolios are held in government debt. Africa’s largest pool of patient capital is, in other words, mostly lending to African governments to cover recurrent spending and service existing debt.


Capability, not permission


Ask why, and the honest answer starts with staffing. As the OECD notes, most African funds lack in-house teams able to price infrastructure risk, run diligence on an unlisted company, or sit on the other side of a negotiation from an experienced fund manager. A trustee board that cannot evaluate a toll-road concession is not being cautious when it declines one; it is being accurate about its own capacity.


This is a solvable problem, but it is solved by unglamorous instruments. Pooled diligence vehicles let several funds share the cost of expertise none can afford alone. First-loss tranches make an unfamiliar asset class survivable on a first attempt. Trustee training that regulators actually fund rather than merely recommend. None of it is a policy announcement. All of it is a line item.


The second answer is incentive, and it is harder. Treasury bills pay well, settle predictably, and have never cost a trustee their job. An underperforming government bond is a market condition. An underperforming private placement is a decision with a name attached to it. Until that asymmetry is addressed directly through how trustees are appointed, indemnified and assessed, raising the ceiling higher simply widens a door nobody is walking through …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Kidus Lemma
title: Once bitter enemies Amhara, Tigray reach understandings in fight against Ethiopian govt
content:
In mid-August, the leader of the Amhara insurgency fighting to overthrow Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed made a surprising announcement. 


The collection of armed Amhara movements fighting in the country’s northwest under the unified Fano umbrella would join an alliance of seven other anti-government groups across the country, Fano leader Zemene Kassie

told

 the Swiss publication, Le Temps.

 


What makes the move surprising is that the alliance includes members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), whom the Amhara forces that make up the Fano fought against during the 2020-2022 war.


In addition to the TPLF, the alliance includes forces from Gumuz, Oromo, the Berta people and Somalia, Zemene said. 


At the national level, the fight between Ethiopian oppositional groups and the government comes against the backdrop of a struggle over the future of the country’s multinational federal system and state’s right to self-determination. 


However, this tension has a larger regional dynamic given Ethiopia’s involvement in the war in Sudan and its expressed desire to secure access to the Red Sea either by diplomatic coup or by force. 


While fighting between the Fano and the Ethiopian government has transformed much of the Amhara Region into an active war zone since late 2023, the beginning of August saw clashes between TPLF forces and the Ethiopian military that threatened to transform long standing simmering tensions between the groups into an active war. 


An African Union diplomat based in Addis Ababa told

Mada Masr

 at the time that any expansion of the fighting in Tigray would have an impact on the calculations of every regional actor because the borders linking Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea are no longer merely dividing lines between states.

 They now form part of an interconnected regional security system in which domestic wars and geopolitical interests overlap, the diplomat added, making any new outbreak of fighting in Tigray a potential factor in reshaping the security landscape of the entire East African region.


The government has responded to the early August clashes with increased military activity. 


In a statement issued on Friday, the Tigray regional government

warned

the international community that the region is nearing “another catastrophic war.”

 


An economic and security blockade has escalated following clashes that broke out on August 1, the statement added, with air strikes and artillery shelling hitting civilian areas, causing casualties and destruction and disrupting cultural activities.


In an interview with Oromia Broadcasting Network on August 7, Abiy criticized the TPLF leadership, accusing it of clinging to outdated political methods and forging alliances that he said threaten stability. 


TPLF deputy chair Amanuel Assefa pointed to a strike on August 20, when a drone

hit

a residential area in Mekelle, Tigray’s capital.

 Residents speaking to Mada Masr confirmed the strike and said several homes were damaged.


Medical sources at Mekelle’s Ayder Specialized Hospital said 13 people were brought in with injuries following the strike, including five women and children, with three in serious condition. The injured ranged in age from two to 60, the sources said.


Tigrayan authorities also said a second strike hit near Mekelle University, though there is no confirmed information on casualties or damage as of the time of publishing.


The strike on Mekelle came only days after another attack that Tigrayan authorities attributed to the Ethiopian military, where a drone struck a farmers’ training center in the Dandera village, about 15 km from Mekelle, on August 18.


Site of drone strike in Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. August 20. Source: Tigray Communications Affairs Bureau via Facebook


While the government hit Tigray, Fano forces continued to secure strategic wins against the Ethiopian military. 


Fano forces in the Wollo provinces of Amhara – which borders southern Tigray — have

claimed

 significant military victories in the past week along the Raya and Ambasel fronts, capturing strategic cities, highway corridors and key positions beyond the Awash River.

 


Fano forces seized the cities of Robit and Aradum and moved within three km of the city of Kobo. Fano troops also took control of the main Waja-Kobo asphalt highway, a critical transit corridor leading to Addis Ababa. 


And on the Ambasel front, Fano forces ambushed government troops moving from Wuchale …

author: The Elephant
title: Bishop. Francis Omondi – The Curious Case of Kenyan Theologies
content:
A central and ongoing theological question in Kenya is the relationship between theology and public and political life, and the kinds of realities and lexicons that this dynamic has produced within the public square. Bishop Francis Omondi talks to The Elephant.

author: Hezron Ochiel
title: When AI Explains African Crises, Local Knowledge Is Barely Visible
content:
Ask any AI tool about the humanitarian situation in Africa, and you will get all sorts of answers in seconds. Then check closely where those answers come from, and you will be left mesmerised.


That very question led me to examine 1,083 verifiable citations used by ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek and Perplexity when answering humanitarian questions about ten African countries. The results revealed that only 5.5% of the citations came from organisations based in the country being discussed, while 68.8% came from United Nations agencies or other multilateral organisations. In other words, the crisis may be local, let’s say in Sudan or Kenya, but the institutions most visible when AI explains it are usually international.


For years, humanitarian localisation or simply put, the shifting of power and resources to local actors in affected countries, has focused on who receives funding, who implements programmes and who participates in decisions. The

Grand Bargain

, for example, committed major humanitarian actors to increasing support for local and national responders. Yet recent analysis by

ODI Global

 shows that large gaps remain between localisation commitments and funding practice.


As AI becomes an alternative way people learn about crises, another dimension is worth examining: Whose knowledge gets seen?


A new layer of humanitarian power


The

African Humanitarian AI Citation Index

 examined questions about Burkina Faso, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan. The questions covered conflict, displacement, food insecurity, health emergencies, water and sanitation, climate shocks, humanitarian access, protection, livelihoods and humanitarian response.


My interest was not simply whether the AI answers were accurate. I wanted to see which organisations appeared as the sources behind those answers. I wanted to see which organisations appeared as the sources behind those answers. Those sources can shape where people look next and, eventually, which organisations they come to see as authoritative.


And, I wanted to see which organisations appeared as the sources behind those answers. In this study, visibility simply refers to which organisations were actually cited. That visibility was concentrated among a relatively small group of organisations.


The five most-cited knowledge producers accounted for 40.3% of all verifiable citations, while the top ten accounted for 58.8%. UNICEF was cited most often, followed by UNHCR, OCHA/Humanitarian Country Team products, OCHA and the International Organisation for Migration. Their prominence is understandable as these organisations publish extensively. In addition, they maintain established websites and archives, and have long-standing authority within the humanitarian system.


The more important question is why credible sources closer to the crises themselves remain so much harder to see.


Kenya: an interesting contrast


The country results were not uniform. Of the 60 country-local citations identified across the ten-country dataset, 31 came from Kenyan sources. Kenya alone accounted for more than half of all local citations found in the study. Nigeria also recorded relatively stronger local visibility.


The picture changed sharply elsewhere. Among 100 verifiable citations concerning the Democratic Republic of the Congo, I did not identify a single citation from an organisation based in the country. Sudan also recorded no country-local citation in its recoverable set, while Somalia recorded only one.


I cannot say from this study exactly why those differences occurred. Language is likely to play a part. So might publishing practices, search visibility, website authority, technical accessibility and the way organisations structure and attribute their information, as well as the fact that a large number of humanitarian organisations operate out of Nairobi as their regional office.


What the findings do show is that local visibility is not equally weak everywhere. That raises the next question: Why is locally produced knowledge easier for AI systems to find and cite in some African countries than in others?


Kenya provides a useful place to begin looking for answers.


Being online does not always mean being visible


African organisations already produce a great deal of knowledge through

government data, local reporting, university research, civil society documentation and humanitarian field …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Warraq residents demonstrate to protest ‘state ignoring legitimate demands’
content:
Hundreds of Warraq Island residents held a protest march on Tuesday, after the head of the authority tasked with developing the island failed to respond to demands they submitted last week, one of the participants in the march told Mada Masr.


Hundreds of residents gathered in the street on Tuesday morning, on the deadline they had given authorities to respond to demands they submitted last week, including that they be granted lands within the state development project, according to the participant as well as videos published by other residents who attended the march.


The crowd then marched toward the New Warraq City Development headquarters, where a heavy security deployment awaited them. Security officials told them that the head of the authority asked for a small group to enter for negotiations. 


The protestors refused, instead demanding that the authority’s head come down to meet them, in an attempt to get a direct response to the demands they had already submitted in writing.


The resident who took part in Tuesday’s march said the authority head’s refusal to come down and meet the residents sparked anger among many of them, but that they kept it in check out of their keenness to keep the protest peaceful. 


But it showed “a lack of consideration, especially since he didn’t meet us when we came to hand over the demands,” the resident said.


The same sentiment was clear at the protest. “Nobody has paid us any attention,” one of the protesters

called

 out to the assembled crowd. “At this moment, we register our objection to the state’s disregard for our legitimate and just demands by saying just one thing: God is sufficient for us, and he is the best disposer of all affairs,” indicating the group’s loss of faith in the authorities’ seriousness. 


The residents then continued their peaceful protest march along the route that had been agreed to in advance. While the march had been planned without chants, still, the residents raised similar cries of “God is sufficient for us” and “one hand.”


At the end of the march, the residents agreed to meet again on Friday to discuss their next steps, and raised the possibility of disrupting ongoing development work on the island.


The residents had submitted a list of demands to the authority on August 18, foremost among them that they be allocated a plot of land within the island’s redevelopment area, where residents who have chosen to stay could build their own homes, according to a defined timeline, with clear and specific implementation mechanisms and fair conditions. They also put forward other demands concerning living and security conditions on the island.


The group handed their written demands to the authority’s deputy chair at the time, with the head elsewhere with another group of Warraq residents, inspecting one of the island’s schools, supposedly to assess potential upgrades.


The resident described to Mada Masr the authority head’s meeting with that group as part of security attempts to “divide.”


One of the people in the group that did not join Tuesday’s march said there were some who had not attended the recent meeting that produced the list of demands. The group who went with the authority head on his school visit opposes holding marches to the authority’s offices, they told Mada Masr. Instead, they have been trying to communicate with officials at the authority and pressure them to implement “as many things as possible that would allow us to keep living on the island,” they continued, adding that they are convinced the government would not agree to give residents land on the island to replace their homes.


The source pointed to what they saw as officials responding to some of the residents’ service-related demands, including bringing back sewage pumping trucks and beginning to clear demolition waste that had piled up along the island’s roads.


Those same measures were described by the resident who took part in Tuesday’s march as “painkillers that don’t work anymore.”


“Some people come and tell you, ‘We brought services,’ when they are our rights that were taken away from us in the first place,” they said. “They’re moving to get the land, so I’m demanding the land.” 


The island has seen a spike in

tensions and incidents between residents and security forces

 in recent weeks, as residents face restrictions on the delivery of construction and building materials.

 


The restrictions, tightening over the nine years since the government …

author: Joseph Winters
title: Big Oil Is Spending Record Amounts to Stop California From Regulating It
content:
The industry poured over $17 million into fighting climate and worker-safety legislation in the first half of 2026.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The fossil fuel industry isn’t just raking in record profits amid the war with Iran. In California, it’s also spending big to oppose climate and worker-safety legislation.

According to analyses by a coalition of environmental groups called the Last Chance Alliance, oil and gas companies spent more than $17 million on California lobbying during the first half of 2026. That includes $10.3 million during the first quarter — a new record for the sector — and another $6.8 million during Q2.

Much of the spending was directed against legislation proposing new costs and liabilities for the fossil fuel industry, like a state bill that would make companies pay for rebuilding following climate-intensified natural disasters. But other bills targeted were more milquetoast, seeking to clarify existing workplace-safety laws and ensure more thorough reporting of cleanup costs when oil companies want to decommission projects.

Faraz Rizvi, campaign and policy director for the nonprofit Asian Pacific Environmental Network — a member of the Last Chance Alliance — criticized companies for “aggressively lobbying” against straightforward measures to protect communities and boost transparency. “They’re not actors that have consumers’ or communities’ interests at heart,” he told Grist.

Last Chance Alliance pulled the data from mandatory reporting to the California secretary of state. The top spenders in the oil-and-gas lobbying category included the Western States Petroleum Association, which spent $4.3 million over the first half of the year; Chevron, whose spending amounted to $3.7 million; and Phillips 66, an oil refiner that spent just over half a million dollars. Much of the money went to consultants and alleged “front groups” that present themselves as grassroots operations but are funded by the fossil fuel industry, like Californians for Energy Independence.

One big target of the sector’s lobbying was California’s cap-and-invest program, which requires companies to pay for a finite — and declining — number of emissions permits each year. The program covers roughly 80 percent of California’s economy and is considered critical to achieving the state’s climate targets, including carbon neutrality by 2045. Earlier this year, oil and gas interests successfully lobbied regulators to green-light a mechanism that could make a vast pool of free pollution permits available to fossil fuel companies. If finalized, the plan could deprive the state of billions in funding that would have otherwise gone toward public transit and housing. The change is currently facing a legal challenge from environmental groups and objections from some Democratic lawmakers.

The sector also fought a bill, currently awaiting passage by the state Senate, to extend California’s Displaced Oil and Gas Workers Fund. Established under a 2022 law, the $30 million fund distributes grants to help oil and gas industry workers transition to new careers. According to one estimate, the fund has already helped 600 people find new lines of work, and supporters have been discussing the potential for new forms of support, including wage replacement during transition periods and financial support during apprenticeships.

Other pending bills that oil companies lobbied against propose creating a task force on safe staffing guidelines for oil refineries; preventing fossil fuel companies from abandoning methane-leaking oil wells; and adding new safety and public comment requirements for offshore oil pipelines. One bill would force companies to submit formal retirement plans before they shutter their oil refineries. The bill follows the closure of a Phillips 66 refinery in L.A. County that environmental groups claim was poorly handled.

A number of the targeted bills have been defeated, giving the oil and gas industry a series of wins. These include SB 1245, which sought to stabilize California’s gas supply, and SB 982, which addressed California’s home insurance crisis. The latter bill would have allowed the state attorney general to sue fossil fuel companies for damages following climate-related disasters like wildfires. It was meant to help pay for skyrocketing property insurance, disaster mitigation, and other …

author: Randi Beers
title: Preaching in a sealskin church
content:
When Rev. Edmund James Peck – Uqammak to the Inuit – and his assistant Joseph Parker arrived on Blacklead Island in Cumberland Sound off the east coast of Baffin Island in the summer of 1894, they took up their quarters in a building that had been provided to them by the Scottish whaling company operating there.


The building was nothing more than a shack, only 200 square feet in size. They had to live in it and cram their year’s supply of perishable goods into it. 


Although there were a number of Scottish whalers on the island, Peck and Parker had come to minister to the Inuit. Some time after their arrival, Peck took a census and found that there were 171 people living on the small island, in some 40 tents.


Immediately the two missionaries established a routine which they generally followed rigidly unless they were travelling.

Much of that routine centred around the learning of Inuktitut.


Peck already spoke the language, from his almost two decades of missionary work on the Quebec coast, but Parker was new to the North and to the language. Peck had not only to learn the nuances of the Blacklead Island dialect that differentiated it from that of Quebec, but also to instruct Parker in the basics of the language. The routine, which required strict self-discipline, was as follows:


“Rise 6:45 a.m., light fires, prepare breakfast; breakfast 8 a.m., prayers 8:30 a.m.; study of Eskimo language with Mr. Parker from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m.; visiting and preparing Eskimo addresses from 10 a.m. to noon. Then came the preparation of dinner. Dinner 1 p.m., private reading and study from 2 p.m. to 3 p.m., school for children from 3 p.m. to 4:15 p.m., visiting and exercise from 4:15 p.m. to 5:30 p.m., tea 5:30 p.m.; after tea, prepare for evening meeting, which is at 7:30 p.m.; after the meeting, study of the language with Eskimos; family prayer at 10 p.m.; then private reading and devotion till 10:45 p.m. This ended the day and bed had been earned.” 


The cramped quarters the two men shared were too small to accommodate many visitors, and they badly needed a place of worship.


The solution to their problem was ingenious, and it was provided by the Blacklead Inuit themselves. They constructed a large tent of sealskin. Indeed it was so large that Peck referred to it as a sealskin “tabernacle.” 


Peck wrote: “Our church – if such it can be called – is 20 feet long and about 10 feet wide. It is made principally of sealskins sewn together, which skins are stretched on a frame and seats are placed inside on which the people sit in rows.”


In a letter to the Church Missionary Society, he wrote, “When I mention the encouraging fact that the whole structure was erected, and to a great measure planned, by the Eskimos themselves, friends will readily see that we have every reason to thank God, and toil on for his people’s salvation without doubt or despondence.”


Peck held his first service in the sealskin church on Sunday, Oct. 7. For him, it was “a very happy but wearing day.”


In his journal, he wrote that “we visited the people from tent to tent, and invited them to come to our opening meeting. Many came, and they joined heartily in the few hymns they knew.” 


This was the humble beginning of Peck’s missionary activity on Blacklead Island, an era that would last through four two-year stints, each punctuated by a year’s furlough in England.


In 1905 Peck finally left Blacklead for good, leaving the mission without a white missionary, but in the capable hands of the Inuit that he and his colleagues had instructed and inspired.


Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: ‘Really healing’: Powwow regalia lending library supports dancers in Anishinaabe Aki
content:
Tisha Duncan with the Wabinoong Regalia Collective booth set-up behind her.

Photo by Tisha Duncan


Tisha Duncan was 19 years old when she had the idea to start a lending library of powwow regalia in Anishinaabe Aki.


She wanted to give free access to regalia for those who wanted to dance at powwows but might be facing barriers — such as young people dancing for the first time, and older people returning to the circle.


So the Wabinoong Regalia Collective began with the goal in mind to reduce financial and social barriers to participation and cultural healing for Indigenous people across northern Ontario.


“So, I had just gotten my driver’s license, I just got in my car, I made it work,” said Duncan, who is now 21.


The member of Bearskin Lake First Nation, an Anishininiw (Oji-Cree) community, was born in Sioux Lookout and grew up in Thunder Bay.


She said her vision for Wabinoong Regalia Collective was inspired by the work of the

Siletz Regalia Closet

, a lending library for Indigenous powwow regalia operating out of “Salem, Oregon.”


Duncan said she had Indigenous Youth in particular in mind — as they are the fastest growing population in “Canada” and facing a crisis of high suicide rates.


“Dancing is like really healing,” Duncan said, adding that “feel good” chemicals get released when moving to the drum beat.


“I think it’s really important to allow Youth to experience that kind of healing.”


‘Just go do it’


Eternity Neekan, a 22-year-old from Mishkeegogamang Ojibway Nation, works for the Wabinoong Regalia Collective.


Neekan initially met and became friends with Duncan through while they were both doing mentorship work with the Regional Multicultural Youth Council in Thunder Bay. 


When she first heard her talk about her idea to start a regalia collective, she recalled urging Duncan to “Just go do it.”


Soon after, Duncan made a call-out for regalia donations. And, in the summer of 2025, she showed up at Whitesand First Nation’s powwow by herself with only a handful of outfits to share, and no booth. 


Now, in their second summer of operations this year, Wabinoong has a team who travels together with a full vendor set-up which includes a changeroom, full-length mirror, a rack full of regalia, and a banner which bears their name, Wabinoong Regalia Collective.


Members of the Wabinoong Regalia Collective at a powwow in northern Ontario. Photo by the Wabinoong Regalia Collective


The group has been able to get powwow committees to waive vendor fees once a committee understands their purpose. 


This has helped them to stretch their limited budget even further.


The Wabinoong Regalia Collective has been able to operate through various grants and donations. 


Duncan estimated that they’ve supported more than 200 rentals in their first year of operations alone. They have also occasionally gifted regalia to those in great need.


As part of their work, they take Youth to powwows, and hire them to work the Wabinoong Regalia Collective booth — paying wages through Canada Summer Jobs grants, which gives them work experience.


The experience has given Youth opportunities to grow confidence and connect with a wide range of people beyond their community at home.


“It’s really fun, like taking Youth to powwows as well, and it’s just a great thing to be involved with. And it makes me feel good. It makes … everyone who rents feel good,” Neekan said. 


“We do that work so we can provide these Youth with their opportunity to engage with their culture.”


One Youth who has been with Wabinoong since the first summer, Neveah Yellowhead, from Nibinamik First Nation, said that working and volunteering with the collective has been one of her favourite things to do each year.


“I get confident in my social skills by how interactive it gets and how much people come to ask questions and give praise,” she wrote. 


“Overall, this collective has made me into someone I’ve dreamt to be, and has shown me experiences in such situations as helping others to pursue their love for dancing.”


A jingle dress donation


Much of the collective’s regalia collection has grown thanks to community generosity. Since 2025, they’ve amassed more than 40 outfits.


Jingle dresses are the most abundant within their collection because they tend to be easier to source. 


“Our biggest donation was 28 jingle dresses,” said Duncan, who mentioned that a woman named Karen Perry was the donor who had gathered the dresses over many years …

author: Mandeep Tiwana
title: Why solidarity is vital to freeing imprisoned human rights defenders
content:
This article

Why solidarity is vital to freeing imprisoned human rights defenders

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Every Aug. 30, the world marks the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances. Beneath the official statements and solemn commemorations lies a stark, unsettling reality: the practice of making people vanish — and holding them in silence away from the world — remains a favored tactic for powerful regimes seeking to crush dissent. The goal of authoritarian states is to cut dissenters off from the outside world until public attention fades. 


Yet as

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani highlighted

 during a global leadership summit last month, solidarity is far more than a moral sentiment; when organized effectively, it acts as a concrete strategy to pull those trapped in state-enforced shadows back into the light. 


Six years ago, when CIVICUS, a global alliance dedicated to strengthening citizen action and civil society, launched the

Stand As My Witness campaign

, we made that exact wager: that the surest way to protect an imprisoned or disappeared defender is public visibility. In practice, that means turning quiet solidarity into loud, coordinated action, sharing their stories, mobilizing petitions, amplifying their voices across borders, and forcing governments to act. The objective is simple: to make their continued detention impossible to ignore.


Since 2020, the campaign has put faces to some 50 detained defenders and helped win freedom for 32 of them. Among them are

Loujain al-Hathloul

, who stood up for women’s right to drive in Saudi Arabia;

Floriane Irangabiye

, who set up a radio station to profile the lives of exiled Burundians; and

Muhammad Ismail

, who spoke out against human rights abuses by security forces in Pakistan. Solidarity works. That is exactly why we cannot stop now. 


Refusing erasure


Authoritarian regimes rely on the quiet assumption that if a prisoner is hidden long enough, the outside world will simply move on. Countering this state-enforced oblivion requires bringing individual names, faces and struggles back into the light.


Khurram Parvez

 has spent decades ensuring that victims of state-enforced disappearances in Kashmir are not forgotten. For that work, the prominent human rights defender was jailed in November 2021 under India’s draconian anti-terror laws. In exposing how security forces made citizens vanish, Parvez became a target of the same machinery of erasure himself.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


In 2023, the U.N. Working Group on Arbitrary Detention declared his imprisonment unlawful. Though an Indian court recently granted him bail after four and a half years without trial, state authorities moved instantly to halt his release. His ongoing ordeal is a reminder that when those who document disappearances are silenced, an entire society loses its voice.


Narges Mohammadi

’s story reveals both the power of witness and its fragility. The Iranian Nobel laureate who has spoken out against torture and the death penalty has been repeatedly arrested, re-sentenced and subjected to periods of incommunicado detention — a form of short-term enforced disappearance designed to cut her off entirely from family, legal counsel and the outside world. 


Her ongoing persecution maps almost exactly onto the world’s attention span: when global pressure was high, she was granted temporary relief; when it eased, authorities placed her in punitive isolation and handed her additional sentences. In May, after collapsing in prison following suspected heart attacks, she was released on medical bail, some 45 pounds lighter and barely recognizable. Her cumulative sentence still stands at 44 years. A conditional release is not freedom, and the threat of return — and total isolation — has never lifted.


Buzurgmehr Yorov

’s decade behind bars illustrates how states turn the justice system itself into a tool of erasure. Arrested in 2015 after taking on targeted political clients and speaking out against their torture, the Tajik lawyer has faced continuous punishment for refusing to stay silent. Held incommunicado and repeatedly placed in solitary isolation, he has been subjected to secret trials behind closed doors that pushed his sentence out to 2043, when he will be in his 70s. Though the U.N. Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for his immediate release years ago …

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: Women’s Equality Day: Many Gains, Still Work To Do
content:
On August 26, 1920, the 19th Amendment was certified, prohibiting the denial of the right to vote on the basis of sex. More than a century later, Women’s Equality Day commemorates that historic victory and the generations of suffragists who fought to secure it.

Women have won extraordinary gains in the 106 years since the 19th Amendment. But the right to vote was only one of the many rights women fought to secure. For much of US history, women were systematically excluded from political decision-making, denied equal access to education and employment, and treated as legally and economically dependent on men.

Through decades of organizing, litigation, and political action, feminists helped expand women’s access to education and the workplace, challenged sex discrimination, fought for protections against sexual harassment, and won greater economic independence, including the ability to obtain credit in their own names. Feminists also fought for access to contraception and abortion, recognizing that the ability to decide whether and when to have children is fundamental to women’s equality and autonomy.

Those struggles transformed the lives of generations of women. Today, women are outpacing men in college completion across every major racial and ethnic group in the US, while women are running for public office in record numbers. From the ballot box to the classroom, the workplace to the legislature, these gains did not happen by accident. They were won by generations of feminists who refused to accept inequality as inevitable. Even as women continue to break barriers and make historic progress, those hard-won gains are not guaranteed.

Yet Women’s Equality Day does not mean that women have achieved equality.

“I never thought that in the US we’d have people arguing to go back to the 19th century,” said Feminist Majority Foundation President and co-founder Eleanor Smeal. “It’s the 21st.”

Today, hard-won rights are once again under attack. The right to make decisions about our own bodies has been stripped away from millions of women since the Supreme Court overturned Roe. Across the country, abortion bans are forcing women to continue pregnancies against their will, while attacks on contraception and other reproductive health care threaten to further limit women’s control over their own lives. Taking that decision away is an attempt to take that power away as well.

Even the rights commemorated by Women’s Equality Day are being questioned. Some have openly advocated for restricting women’s voting for “household voting” that could give husbands greater control over how families vote. The fact that taking away women’s independent voting power is being discussed at all is a reminder that hard-won rights cannot be taken for granted.

“We never thought bad things would happen again,” said Kathy Spillar, executive director of Feminist Majority Foundation. “We demand equality, no less—but we must ensure that there is equality.”

That fight includes securing the Equal Right Amendment to explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex in the Constitution. Although the ERA has been fully ratified by the required 38 states, it has yet to be recognized as part of the Constitution. The majority of states have also adopted some form of constitutional protection for equal rights based on sex—or State ERA’s—but protections vary across the country.

Women’s Equality Day should be a celebration of how far women have come, but not a declaration of victory. We can celebrate the suffragists who fought for the ballot, the feminists who expanded women’s access to education and economic independence, and the generations of women who broke barriers in politics and public life. But equality is not guaranteed. We must continue fighting for reproductive freedom, an end to violence against women, equal opportunity and representation, and constitutional equality. Women’s Equality Day is a reminder of what feminists have won, and why we must keep fighting to protect it.
