title: Artillery attack on Suwayda kills two people
content:
According to information reported by the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR), a mortar shell fired from areas under the control of Syria’s interim government struck neighborhoods in western Suwayda.


The attack killed a woman named Asya, who had been forcibly displaced from the Jazira region and was working on agricultural land in Suwayda, as well as the tractor driver. Two other people were reportedly injured in the attack.


Following the attack, the bodies of those killed and the injured were taken to hospitals.

author: Micah Rieder
title: The Polyrhythm of Israeli Entitlement in Thailand
content:
IN RECENT WEEKS, the polyrhythm of Israeli entitlement in Thailand has practically saturated the news cycle. A tall order, given a school-shooting massacre, a number of copycat incidents, and near-vertical escalations of separatist violence in the south.

Most notable among the tunes in rotation: a confrontation over a zoo on the island of Koh Samui, where a Thai-French couple refused entry to a group of Israelis. By the time the smoke cleared –and there was actual smoke–Israelis had made death threats, a 500,000 baht bounty had been placed on the couple running the business, and the Israeli ambassador had met with provincial officials to insist Israeli tourists be protected, just in time for the Thai-French family’s home in France to be set ablaze.

That the embers of Israeli-linked fires in South America and Europe have made landfall in Thailand (by way of France) is, oddly, the cheap punchline here. More interesting is that someone determined that the Thai-French couple owned a house on the other side of the world, then tracked down and targeted it. The A to B of that is no small task, and it went down with unlikely speed and accuracy. In other words, this was not some impulsive, retaliatory tantrum. It involved considerable intelligence-gathering and logistics coordination.

Given that, it bears mentioning that the very spyware Thai journalists and democracy activists have found running on their phones in recent years was developed in Tel Aviv. All of which makes one particular development in this saga rather conspicuous. Thai Mai Thon (“Impatient Thais”) –Thailand’s own Proud Boy-esque nationalist goon squad, best known for assaulting democracy activists in Bangkok– is now positioning itself as something of a cavalry against Israeli entitlement.

Why is that conspicuous? Pull up a chair.

SINCE 2010, Thailand has had an official arrangement with Israel, exporting farmworkers to compensate for shortages resulting from Israeli restrictions on Palestinian movement. In practice, this pipeline has existed since the early 1990s. The capture and death of Thai nationals on Oct. 7th was the direct result of this program and, indeed, Hamas seemed aware of it. Thais who evaded capture reported hearing Hamas militants calling to them in Thai, as they hid.

By that time, hundreds of Thai migrant workers had already died on Israeli farms, likely from heat exhaustion and reportedly brutal working hours – all of which appear to have been chalked up to “arrhythmia”.

None of which was terribly interesting to Thai nationalists. At any point. At any level.

Getting to Israel involves massive payments to agencies that broker migrant worker entry; families often take on debt in the process, and remain liable for those debts when the workers die. Meanwhile, when Thai women farm workers in Israel were surveyed, 100% of respondents reported experiencing sexual assault. Thailand has not meaningfully addressed any of this. Certainly, the latter stat has not meaningfully informed visa policy per Israelis entering the country, or the risks they pose to the local population.

On this point, the silence of Thai nationalists has been, rather predictably, deafening.

The harvest of that inaction has been similarly foreseeable. In the last year, Israeli tourists have made Thai headlines attacking hospital workers, stealing from Thai businesses, and in one particularly illustrative incident, defecating on a cafe floor. All while establishing de facto colonies in places like Pai, Koh Phangan, and Phuket.

The Thai nationalists presently submitting petitions to the Israeli embassy and peacocking on social media? Nowhere to be found.

So much so that grassroots Thai anger at Israeli entitlement reached a volume impossible to ignore. For months, a two-pronged government response has been underway. On one side, an overhaul of visa-exempt entry policies long exploited by tourists from a host of countries. As a result, the visa-free sixty days granted to a range of passport-holders since Covid restrictions were lifted has been reduced to thirty. Or so one is to believe, anyway. Sixty-day visa-free stamps have appeared in passports as recently as last week.

On the other side, a crackdown on illegal, foreign-run businesses and land deals has revealed a number of shocking stats. On Phuket, some 361 businesses now face investigation for using nominee structures to appear Thai-owned after a confrontation with the local Chabad House. Among them, ten …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica?
content:
Oceanagold's mining operations in Didipio, Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya have dried up the sources of water, polluted the environment and crippled the livelihood of farmers. (Photo by John Aaron Mark Macaraeg / Bulatlat)

“The presidential order is apparently intended to assure potential investors that national government mechanisms are in place to respond to Pax Silica’s mineral requirements.”

CAGAYAN DE ORO — Concerned groups expressed alarm following the issuance of an executive order establishing a policy framework for developing the critical minerals industry.

The International League of Peoples’ Struggles (ILPS) Philippines and the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center (LRC) suspected that Executive Order (EO) No. 122 issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on August 18 is linked to the United States (U.S.)-led Pax Silica initiative that aims to establish a 1,600-hectare industrial hub in New Clark City in Tarlac.

The site is being promoted as an economic security zone that would strengthen shared supply chains in critical minerals, semiconductors, electronics, and other goods.

Arnold Padilla, ILPS Philippines secretary-general, said that the order’s issuance happened ahead of the upcoming Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investors Forum in September. “The presidential order is apparently intended to assure potential investors that national government mechanisms are in place to respond to Pax Silica’s mineral requirements.”

The industrial hub under Pax Silica is set to be built within the LEC.

Under the EO, a national exploration and mineral reservation program is set to be implemented by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) of the Department of the Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). The program aims to identify and evaluate new critical mineral deposits.

Critical minerals, under the order, refers to “essential inputs for clean energy transition technologies, advanced manufacturing, digital infrastructure, national defense, and other strategic industries necessary to promote industrialization, energy security, economic resilience, and sustainable development.”

There is also a strict implementation of the “Use it or Lose it” policy, directing the DENR to enforce the timely and responsible development of critical mineral mining tenements. Those tenements that are found to be in material non-compliance without valid justification shall be subject to cancellation.

Moreover, areas covered by cancelled, expired, relinquished, surrendered, or freed-up critical mining tenements may be considered as critical mineral reservations, subject to verification and assessment.

In coordination with DENR-MGB and other concerned government agencies, the Privatization and Management Office is also directed “to accelerate the disposition and privatization of all government-owned critical mineral mining assets.”

The order also directed the reorganization of the Mining Industry Coordinating Council (MICC) and streamlining and digitalizing the mining permitting process through a virtual one-stop shop.

In a statement, lawyer Mai Taqueban, LRC executive director, expressed concern about the inclusion of critical minerals for advanced manufacturing, digital infrastructure, and national defense in implementing a national exploration and mineral reservation program.

“This squarely frames our critical minerals policy within the Pax Silica framework, and confirms suspicions of the intent to link domestic mining and minerals processing to the ‘war production’ value chain,” she said.

Read: ‘Pax Silica’ initiative seen as war production, environment destruction

She stressed that the EO opens up nine million hectares of potential areas having mineral deposits, as reported by the Philippine Board of Investments, to mining exploration and reservation. “This represents a potential 1,000% increase of mining land area compared to the present total hectarage of approved mining projects.”

More than 790,000 hectares of land in the country are covered by large-scale mining contracts, according to Acting Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna.

On February 4, the Philippine government and the U.S. signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to diversify global critical mineral supply chains. The partnership reportedly provides a framework to have stable and resilient supply and value chains in critical minerals and rare earths in both countries.

author: rti_admin
title: The Vanishing Government School: Caste, Class, and the Quiet Dismantling of India’s Public Education Promise
content:
“The debate over school closures is not about infrastructure alone. It is about deciding whose children deserve a neighbourhood school and whose education can be sacrificed in the name of efficiency and reform.”

Abstract: Over the past decade, India has witnessed the closure or merger of more than 93,000 government schools—a transformation officially justified as administrative “rationalisation” and educational efficiency. Yet this process is unfolding unevenly, with its greatest consequences borne by Dalit, Adivasi, OBC, and poor Muslim children, who rely overwhelmingly on neighbourhood government schools. Drawing upon the latest NITI Aayog report, UDISE+ data, parliamentary records, constitutional provisions, and recent field reporting, this article argues that school consolidation is not merely a technical reform but a restructuring of educational access with profound implications for social justice. It contends that the shrinking of public schooling undermines the constitutional promise of equality and revives an older hierarchy in which quality education increasingly becomes the privilege of those who can afford it, while the marginalised are left to negotiate longer distances, greater exclusion, and diminished educational opportunity.

On 17 June 2026, officials in Uttar Pradesh’s Gorakhpur district issued a routine administrative order directing the merger of Primary School Mirza Babu with another government school located several kilometres away. Similar directives soon appeared across Mathura and other districts, instructing authorities to identify schools with fewer than twenty students for consolidation.

Such notifications rarely attract national attention. They are framed as bureaucratic necessities intended to optimise resources and improve educational quality. Yet behind these seemingly ordinary administrative decisions lies one of the most significant transformations of India’s public education system since Independence.

According to information placed before Parliament, the number of government schools declined from 11.07 lakh in 2014–15 to nearly 10.13 lakh in 2024–25, representing a loss of more than 93,000 schools over a decade. The scale is staggering: approximately twenty-five government schools disappeared every day for ten consecutive years. Simultaneously, the share of children studying in government schools has steadily declined while enrolment in private institutions has continued to expand. These trends are documented not only in parliamentary records but also in the NITI Aayog’s 2026 report, School Education System in India: Temporal Analysis and Policy Roadmap for Quality Enhancement, which presents perhaps the most comprehensive recent assessment of India’s schooling landscape.

The closure of a school, however, cannot be understood merely as the disappearance of a building. For millions of children belonging to Dalit, Adivasi, OBC, and economically disadvantaged Muslim communities, the neighbourhood government school represents the first—and often the only—meaningful encounter with the Indian state. It is where constitutional promises of equality, citizenship, and social mobility become tangible. When such institutions disappear, the burden does not fall equally across society. Middle-class families frequently possess alternatives: private schools, transport, digital learning resources, and supplementary coaching. Marginalised households often possess none of these. Consequently, what appears as administrative efficiency in policy documents frequently translates into educational exclusion on the ground.

This article argues that the ongoing wave of government school mergers represents far more than an exercise in administrative rationalisation. It reflects a broader restructuring of India’s public education system that disproportionately disadvantages historically marginalised communities. By analysing recent evidence from UDISE+, the NITI Aayog report, parliamentary debates, and constitutional provisions, the article asks a fundamental question: Who pays the social cost of educational rationalisation? It contends that the answer lies at the intersection of caste, class, geography, and state responsibility.

Public Education and the Unfinished Democratic Project

The contemporary debate on school closures is not an isolated administrative question; it belongs to a much longer history of educational inequality in India. More than a century before the Right to Education became a …

author: Alexis Vassiley
title: Labor’s Secret Harbour by-election loss is ominous
content:
Less than eighteen months ago, Western Australian Corrective Services Minister Paul Papalia comfortably held the seat of Secret Harbour, in Perth’s southern suburbs, with a two-party preferred vote of 61.5 percent in the state election. The by-election on Saturday wasn’t even close. One Nation currently leads 57-43 on a two-party preferred basis with 75 percent of the vote counted.

ON candidate Luke Herdegen’s 39 percent primary vote represents a swing of more than 30 percent to the party since last year. Labor’s primary vote plummeted to less than 25 percent, for a negative swing of 22 percent.

Labor’s campaign was utterly tone deaf. Papalia, who retired last month, triggering the by-election, told the

West Australian

days before the election: ‘‘We live in the best state in the best country on planet Earth, and part of the reason for that is good, solid, responsible government”. Anthony Albanese flew to Perth, not to campaign in the election, but for a $10,000-a-head fundraising dinner in a mansion on a street nicknamed “millionaire’s row”.

The party’s candidate selection was no better. Georgia Tree, a government relations advisor to Woodside Energy, was parachuted into what was considered “safe” territory. She previously worked for Federal Resources Minister Madeline King. Tree tried to leverage her working-class roots, saying how important Medicare and TAFE were to her parents. But all she could muster was a pathetic $100 fuel payment for motorists as her answer to the cost-of-living crisis.

Labor threw its all at the campaign, spending more than $400,000 (of which $14,850 came from Woodside). The premier seemingly never left the candidate’s side, while government MPs from all across Perth doorknocked. Labor also spent millions on a pork-barrelling spree and promised to finally start work on a train station they first promised ten years ago. But it was to no avail.

Despite what WA Labour tells itself, voters are not happy. A Demos poll in late August asked respondents if the state government was doing a good or bad job managing particular issues. Its

best

 result was 0 percent for “net good job” (i.e. the same percentage thought it was doing a good and bad job) for education and schools. On the cost-of-living, net good job was negative 56 percent; for housing it was negative 57 percent.

Indeed, the health and education systems are in crisis. The housing situation is thrown into stark relief on Memorial Drive, in the neighbouring Rockingham electorate, where hundreds of homeless people sleep in tents and caravans. Yet funding can be found to build housing for 1,200 defence personnel from the US and UK. In fact, Labor governments are spending billions of dollars on nearby military facilities at HMAS Stirling and the Henderson industrial precinct.

Secret Harbour is one of the least diverse seats in the state. There are fewer immigrants than the state average; those there hail largely from the UK, New Zealand and South Africa. Largely working class, more people have vocational qualifications than university degrees.

Gym owner Herdegen’s pitch centred on infrastructure, the cost of living, crime, immigration and housing. He told voters that Labor had neglected the area for too long, and this was an opportunity to send a message. Herdegen’s campaign did not shy away from far-right talking points. One social media video, for instance, talked about “saving the family suburb”, blaming a “population explosion” for ruining the “suburban Australian dream”, featuring white faces and nostalgic music. The One Nation campaign also spent a huge amount.

The Liberals did badly, coming third with around 17 percent of the primary vote (a negative swing of nearly 8 percent. State Liberal leader Basil Zempilas provoked a stoush with the Liberal federal MP for Canning, Andrew Hastie (whose seat overlaps with Secret Harbour), by claiming that a One Nation win would actually be a Liberal “victory”.

The Greens vote held mostly steady at 7.5 percent. The party campaigned on Labor’s neglect of the area, the cost of living, housing and against the AUKUS security pact.

So this was a good night for the racist far-right bigots of One Nation. The orange wave is real. Prior to Secret Harbour, it remained to be seen if One Nation could actually win seats off Labor. They can, and “safe” ones at that. Labor had held Secret Harbour and its previous incarnations since 1989. Only in 2008 and 2025 did Labor candidate need preferences to …

author: Mat Ward
title: The 10 most inspiring new protest albums right now
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for August.

Pro-Palestine protesters from Magan-djin/Brisbane rallied with activists from New South Wales' Northern Rivers at the Queensland border on August 1. They did so to highlight six words - "from the river to the sea" - that are legal in NSW but banned in Queensland. The same day, US protest singer David Rovics released his new album with Magan-djin-based musician - and long-time Green Left contributor - Kamala Emmanuel. It contains a song that, Rovics noted, is illegal in Queensland. On "From The River", they sing: "At the turn of the 20th century, it became a penitentiary, and at home or far away, you can hear them say, from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free." Two days later, British band Massive Attack were banned from Singapore for flying a Palestine flag on stage. Meanwhile, Rovics continued to release AI-generated protest albums as Ai Tsuno, his artificial intelligence alter ago. LISTEN>>>

On the same day Rovics released his latest Ai Tsuno album, the Socialist Alliance released a statement opposing the rapid expansion of AI data centres. A week later, the New York Times said a new Amazon data centre was stoking fears it "would be the most polluting power plant in the US". A fortnight after that, The Washington Post said Republicans had even started attacking Democrats for "being too soft on data centres". Addressing the data centre disgust is the new album from US punks The Carp, released on August 14. On its opening track, they yell: "They're going to put a data centre in your town! They're buying up the farmland in your town!" A week later, investigative journalists revealed the identities of the men behind viral, white, racist AI rapper Danny Bones. British-Jamaican rapper Lava La Rue noted “the irony of giving him a British-Jamaican rapping voice over a Black hip-hop beat". LISTEN>>>

Country-punk musicians Mike And The Molotovs liken people's fear of AI to the horror colonised people have been suffering for centuries at the hands of their invaders. On their new EP, released on August 15, they sing: "How will it feel to be colonised? When the robots come, they won't apologise. How will it feel to be swept away? We're going to find out some day." Just 10 days later, media outlet Quartz reported that US bank JPMorgan was expecting robot demand to surge. "At under $US10 per hour to operate, a humanoid robot undercuts the roughly $US30 hourly cost of a warehouse worker by a significant margin." Meanwhile, a new study estimated the earnings of people who are paying as little as $US10 a month to use music-generating AI platforms trained on humans' stolen work. Topping the list was remixer Cherry 葵 Nightcore, "bringing in an apparent $US2 million" from 941 million YouTube views. LISTEN>>>

Someone who already knows full well how it feels to be colonised, Indigenous rapper Miss Kaninna, released her radical new record on August 21. The groundbreaking Yorta Yorta, Dja Dja Wurrung, Kalkadoon and Yirendali musician was raised by her mother Ruth Langford, who was recently hauled before court for taking part in an anti-logging protest, and grandmother Rosalind Langford, the co-founder of the Aboriginal Information Service, which became the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre. Discussing the album, Miss Kaninna noted she was about to play Mparntwe/Alice Springs, where "you have a complete fuckstorm of white people trying to control Aboriginal people's lives, right down to what we fucking put in our mouths". Two days before the LP's release, Mparntwe town camp resident Eileen Hoosan noted life expectancy became far longer when the Aboriginal community took control of health services from whites. LISTEN>>>

The life expectancy of Aboriginal people in Western Australia is 68.9 years. But the state government defines priority applicants for its Stolen Generations compensation payments as anyone over the age of 85. That means dozens of applicants who were taken from their parents as children are dying before they receive any compensation, The Australian reported on August 27. A fortnight earlier, West Australian Aboriginal rapper Kayps released his debut album, which rails against such injustices. "World sing to the stories of our people before they killed us and poisoned the rest," he raps on …

author: Jerome Small
title: Vic premier’s attack on independent unions is an attack on decent unionism
content:
Organisations that offer workers some choice over who represents their industrial interests should be in the same legal category as violent fascist gangs and listed terrorist organisations. This is the intended effect of

amendments

 to laws governing incorporated associations, introduced into the Victorian parliament in mid-August by new Premier Ben Carroll’s Labor government. 

The law threatens to wipe out the Retail and Fast Food Workers Union (RAFFWU), which is a challenger to Labor’s largest affiliated union—the notoriously right-wing Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA). Much of the media coverage has presented Carroll’s appalling attack on RAFFWU as a straightforward factional payback, after the SDA-aligned faction within the Labor caucus supported Carroll when he rolled Jacinta Allen as premier of Victoria last month. 

Factional favours may well be a factor, but there’s more to it than that. 

As well as being a gift to the SDA leadership, Carroll’s move is part of a nationwide trend for Labor to crack down on any idea that workers should be entitled to seek representation from a union body not currently licensed by the state through the Fair Work Commission. 

Similar legislation

 to the current Victorian bill was passed in Queensland in 2022 under the Labor government of Annastacia Palaszczuk. And the

Australian Financial Review


reported

 in mid-August that Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth, a former SDA organiser, moved amendments to the national Labor platform at July’s national ALP conference “to bind the party to target ‘sham unions’”. According to the

AFR

: “The amendments say Labor will legislate to limit unregistered unions’ participation in industrial matters, including acting as bargaining representatives”.

Labor figures say that the main target of these moves are the so-called “Red” unions set up in recent years. These “Red” unions are indeed a crime against decent, principled unionism. Their main instigator is Graeme Haycroft, who has a long history in the Liberal National Party in Queensland and was a long-time, prominent member of the notorious 1980s union-busting think tank the

HR Nicholls Society

.

But the best remedy against right-wing unions preying on workers is political exposure, along with established unions demonstrating their superiority through organising strikes and industrial action that improve workers’ lives. This is clearly too much work to contemplate for most of today’s union leaders, and would run totally counter to their politics, which emphasises class collaboration rather than class combat. Much easier to just rely on Labor to wipe out any competitors through legal and bureaucratic methods.

It’s not just RAFFWU and the “Red” unions that are affected by Labor’s attacks. For a decade from 2015, the farm workers’ organising team of the United Workers Union conducted a series of effective—in fact,

outstanding

—organising drives among migrant workers on farms. These workers sometimes made use of the provisions in the Fair Work Act that allow workers to nominate independent bargaining agents to represent them at enterprise agreement negotiations. 

This enabled workers to get around the dictates of the Fair Work Commission, which enforces a legal monopoly on union coverage for most industries in Australia. In the case of farms, this state-sanctioned monopoly belonged to the Australian Workers Union, which had done zero organising on farms for decades and was utterly opposed to any other union doing this organising either. 

Removing the ability of workers to appoint an independent bargaining agent in these circumstances, which seems to be the intention of Rishworth’s proposed changes to national industrial laws, would pose a significant problem for workers in situations like this. Migrant farm workers would be able to secure decent representation only by overthrowing the entire national leadership of the AWU, one of the oldest and strongest bureaucratic machines within Australia’s union movement. 

There’s also the case of the

Independent Transport Union

, a breakaway from the Rail, Tram and Bus Union in Victoria. Unlike RAFFWU, the ITU didn’t start as a project of the left, but rather as a sectional breakaway representing train drivers. But regardless of its origins, the ITU has become an effective industrial force within V/Line, Victoria’s regional rail network. The ITU’s existence as an incorporated association is clearly …

author: Cecilia Judge
title: Victory for rank-and-file ticket in Victorian health union election
content:
A group of rank-and-file unionists have ousted the leadership of the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association (VAHPA) in a landslide election. The VAHPA Pulse ticket, made up of rank-and-file union activists, gained almost twice the vote of the incumbents, VAHPA Unity, and won all the positions.

The VAHPA Unity team has controlled the union for fourteen years and was backed by significant anonymous donations. By contrast, VAHPA Pulse, which I am part of, relied for our support on conviction and our reputations as experienced and uncompromising delegates and activists. Our victory is the culmination of many years of hard work and solid rank-and-file union activity.

The outgoing leadership took control of VAHPA with the ticket name “Clean Sweep”. Clean Sweep faced off against cronies of former national secretary Kathy Jackson, who was responsible for disgraceful corruption and whose actions gave bosses and anti-unionists ammunition to attack unions. Defeating them was an important victory.

However, after the new leadership stemmed the haemorrhaging of members and rebranded the union from HSU Branch 3 to the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association to signal the beginning of a new era, there has been little in terms of concrete improvements for allied health workers.

I started working in public health just a few months after Clean Sweep came into office. Coming from the community sector, I was excited at the prospect of better pay and conditions in the health system. Today, members are leaving public health for the community sector for the same reason.

However, it’s not just our pay and conditions that have gone backwards under Clean Sweep. Members have also become increasingly frustrated and angry with the lack of communication and transparency on the part of the leadership, as well as its hostility to rank-and-file activity.

After working on the front lines throughout the pandemic, allied health workers had an enterprise agreement pushed on us in 2022 that contained a pathetic 2 percent pay “rise”. As the cost-of-living crisis intensifies and the workload increases in quantity and complexity, VAHPA members increasingly find themselves unable to remain in the sector, whether for financial reasons or their own mental health, often both.

At the 2023 delegates conference there was hope that the situation facing allied health workers might start to turn around. A new public sector organising team presented its three-year plan to rebuild delegate structures and networks in the lead-up to our next round of bargaining. There seemed to be a willingness to involve members and an understanding of the central role delegates play in not only recruiting members but also helping them become active unionists.

We all left excited. Delegates formed new working groups. In particular, professional reference groups were established to provide a mechanism for different occupational groups within VAHPA to raise their particular issues within the union.  Given VAHPA represents around 50 different professions within the complex health system, this work was vital not only to assist the union organisers to understand the issues on the floor, but also to strengthen our identity and ultimately our industrial confidence. All this work was to help inform our strategy before negotiations began on our next agreement.

These exciting developments were unfortunately short lived. We were told by the union leadership, and directly by the secretary, that this work was undermining and divisive to the union as a whole. Radiation therapists, arguably our most organised profession within the union, had been taking initiative in organising across the state and reaching out to their interstate counterparts to learn from their industrial victories. This was attacked by the leadership, which accused these workers of leaving other professions behind.

The message was clear: the leadership calls the shots.

The 2025 delegate conference was very different. Even friendly attempts by members to connect with each other were responded to aggressively by the leadership. I was rudely shouted at by the secretary on the conference floor after I asked for clarification about staffing. Later, I was attacked by an organiser and a delegate (who ran for assistant secretary on the VAHPA Unity ticket) in front of other delegates when I, on behalf of a core group of rank-and-file delegates, offered to start up a rank-and-file WhatsApp chat to increase …

author: Susan Price
title: Songs of working class struggle:  Les Thomas brings ‘I Remember Everything’ home after British tour
content:
I caught up with Melbourne singer-songwriter Les Thomas, who is back in Australia after a highly successful British tour that took his music from London clubs and Oxford’s Blackwell’s bookshop to the Tolpuddle Martyrs Festival in Dorset.

Thomas travelled to Britain in July with a collection of songs about memory, working lives, history, love and resistance, unsure how they might connect with audiences on the other side of the world.

He needn't have worried. By the time he returned to Melbourne this month, he had performed across England, sold all of his CDs and found his songs had struck a chord in ways he had not anticipated.

Thomas told Green Left that audience members had approached him after shows to talk about their own lives and histories. “Some were moved to tears by the album’s title track, which travels across centuries of violence, struggle and resistance that underscores working class history,” he said.

One of the tour’s most unusual performances was at Blackwell’s Books in Oxford, where Thomas presented his new album I Remember Everything: Songs, Stories and Social History. The bookshop provided a fitting backdrop for songs about personal experiences woven into the fabric of history.

Then there was the Tolpuddle Martyrs Festival — a place where the struggle for workers’ rights changed history.

For Thomas, who has a deep connection with the trade union movement, performing at the festival carried particular significance.

“The Dorset village is synonymous with the six agricultural labourers who were transported to Australia in 1834 after forming a trade union and refusing to accept attempts to cut their wages,” he said.

Thomas performed four times during the festival weekend, from the Radical History school, multiple stages to an impromptu set in the festival bar that scored him an extra festival in North Devon.

The audience response was matched by strong reviews. Americana UK awarded the album four-and-a-half stars, describing it as “an absolute gem which should be studied line by line in schools”. Liverpool Sound and Vision gave it 8.5 out of 10, while Fatea Magazine described the record as “poignantly personal and deeply humanist”.

The album’s appeal is perhaps best explained by the breadth of its historical gaze.

The title song moves through the slave trade, palawa warrior Truganini, the Irish Famine, the Easter Uprising, King Leopold’s Congo, Guernica, Amritsar, the Tolpuddle Martyrs and the struggles of Appalachian mine workers. The vast sweep of history then gives way to personal memory within the much longer human story.

“The Last of the Old Holdens” looks at the disappearance of Australian car manufacturing through the eyes of those who lived through it. “The Life of Eloise” addresses violence against women and the responsibility of men to challenge it. “The Firing Line” confronts the destruction of civilian life in war and calls out the complicity of silence.

But I Remember Everything is not simply a political record. Songs about love, ageing, loss, family and the search for peace sit alongside the politics. Thomas’s insistence that individual lives matter — and that remembering them matters too — underpins the entire album.

Thomas wrote and produced the album, recording with Joshua Jones, Trevayne Fernandez, Justin Olsson, Craig Kelly, Ben Franz and Jason Bunn, with harmony vocals from Trudy Fatnowna Edgeley, Mandy Connell, Jacinta Percy, Kyana, Suzie So Blue and Emmy Ryan. Guus Hoevenaars predominantly mixed the album, with Carra mastering.

The album artwork also reflects Thomas’s preoccupation with history and memory.

Its cover features JMW Turner’s The Slave Ship, the 1840 painting created by the abolitionist artist in response to the Zong massacre, when enslaved Africans were thrown overboard from a British slave ship.

After taking these songs through Britain — and to a festival rooted in the history of the labour movement — Thomas is bringing them back to Melbourne, where they were written and recorded.

I Remember Everything will be released through Oily Rag Records on September 14. Thomas will launch the album with a rare full band celebration at the Northcote Social Club on Sunday September 20, joined by special guests Mandy Connell, Emmy Ryan and Suzie So Blue.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: How politicians and CEOs got addicted to profit
content:
Hooked: Inside the murky world of Australia’s gambling industry

. By Quentin Beresford. NewSouth Publishing; 352 pages; $39.99

“Of all the prime ministers I’ve known, and I’ve known all of them since Menzies, Albanese is the most gambling-captured prime minister I’ve ever seen”, Tim Costello is quoted as saying in Quentin Beresford’s 2025 book

Hooked: Inside the murky world of Australia’s gambling industry

.

Detailing the history of the gambling industry and its tight connection with the Australian political class,

Hooked

 provides the case for meaningful gambling reform, something neither major political party is willing to implement.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026, which passed parliament in August, hardly scratches the surface of an industry that includes sport betting, both at TABs and online, pokies, casinos and more.

Australian gambling losses are now at a staggering

$31.5 billion

 per year, and have been consistently rising since records began in the mid-1970s. The new legislation doesn’t ban advertising or inducements (like free bets or text messages). It doesn’t remove poker machines from our communities. And it leaves the casinos free to continue operating.

Despite being deemed “

the strongest ever gambling reforms”

 by Communications Minister Anika Wells’ office, the bill stops short of seriously impacting the companies making mega-profits. Beresford’s book gives insight into why, despite there being overwhelming popular support for gambling reform, both Labor and Liberal governments have never been willing to do it.

The entrance of the poker machine was a major turning point in the history of gambling in Australia. In New South Wales in 1956, pokies were legalised and rugby league clubs were given the sole right to operate them. These clubs, according to one expert quoted in

Hooked

, “‘subordinated their social agenda to economic interests’ and grew wealthy on the back of poker machines”.

These league clubs were often the centre of the community. In the 1960s, the South Sydney Junior Leagues Club had 45,000 members. It offered facilities and activities that were not always available to working-class people, like squash courts, a swimming pool, lounge and library. But it also had 111 poker machines, with more on order.

The profits that came from these poker machines in clubs all across New South Wales became the key source of income for the rugby clubs. Beresford quotes the CEO of South Sydney, who recalled that they became “fat, dumb and happy” on the profits from the machines. By the end of the 1960s, there were 20,000 poker machines across New South Wales. Today, more than

80,000 are operating across the state

. This is an increase in poker machines that is twice the rate of population increase.

The relationship between the sports codes and the gambling industry has continued apace. After the release of Labor MP Peta Murphy’s report “You Win Some, You Lose More” in 2023 following a Senate inquiry, the “heavyweights of free-to-air TV and the football codes went all-out to lobby the Albanese government to prevent an ad ban”. This is because it’s not just sports clubs that rely heavily on a revenue stream from pokies.

The AFL receives at least $30 million from gambling agencies revenue, and the NRL $50 million.


The NRL still has direct relationships with gambling agencies, with half the clubs sponsored by agencies. The revenue they receive is not taxed, as both institutions are not-for-profits. The free-to-air broadcasters get around

11 percent of their

 revenue from gambling ads. This amounts to $150 million from gambling advertising each year. These relationships mean that there are multiple institutions lobbying the government; the broadcasters, the clubs and the gambling companies themselves.

One chapter in Beresford’s book details the way these lobbying efforts helped to destroy attempts at reforming the industry by Andrew Wilkie, an independent MP from Tasmania. Wilkie had struck up an agreement with then-Prime Minister Julia Gillard, who was returned to power in a minority government with support from the Greens and independents. Wilkie’s main interest was the gambling industry, which had sucked huge amounts of money from Tasmanians via poker machines and the Wrest Point casino in Hobart. This was Australia’s first legal casino, approved by a Labor government in 1968 following a referendum.

Wilkie had previously campaigned against Coles …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Toronto students say One Nation is not welcome in Cessnock
content:
With less than 24-hours’ notice, more than 100 mostly young people organised a vibrant protest on August 28 to show Pauline Hanson and One Nation that they are not welcome in Toronto, NSW.

Toronto High students and Youth Rising (a group that supports Rising Tide) and others others lined the footpath at the Toronto Hotel where Hanson held a $1000-a-head fundraising dinner for One Nation’s Cessnock candidate.

Many decorated themselves as clowns. They created a festive atmosphere, dancing to rap and popular music including “9 to 5” by Dolly Parton, the Macarena and, of course, the Pauline Pantsdown hit “I don't like it”.

There were busts of chanting, including “Racist, sexist, anti-queer, Hanson you’re not welcome here”.

A number of those driving by showed their support, with excited waves, shouts, blowing kisses and vigorously honking their horns.

The NSW Police presence was mild, with occasional requests to ensure a clear passage along the footpath.

Two Toronto High students told me that this was their first protest, and that most people are their school mates. “We're so glad we came; we didn’t think it would make a difference but it did, we just feel so much better and we feel we can change things.”

author: Jessica Abbo
title: The University of Queensland is trying to destroy our student union
content:
This morning at the University of Queensland, hundreds of students protested management’s attacks on our student union. A proposed “transition plan” would result in millions of dollars of students’ money (collected through the Student Services and Amenities Fee) being channelled away from democratically elected student representatives to bureaucrats who answer to the university’s administrators.

This is a huge attack on students’ right to politically organise on campus. Currently, the student union is independent from the university, which gives it the ability to criticise and stand up to the administration when it attacks students. Increasing fees, cutting courses and raising rents on student accommodation are common measures taken by the university to make more money at students’ expense. An independent student union can organise students to oppose attacks like these.

Student unions can also organise campaigns about important political issues students care about, such as supporting Palestine or opposing Pauline Hanson. For example, in 2024, 1,500 students demanded the university cut ties with weapons companies and Israel in a meeting called by the student union. University managers despised this rabble-rousing because it called into question their right to take money from companies facilitating the Gaza genocide. The university views protests like these as harmful to its public image and, therefore, to its ability to do business.

The radical potential of the student union is exactly why the university wants to shut it down. Students standing against injustice and preventing the university from doing whatever it wants is a huge thorn in the side of the university bosses.

Unfortunately, we don’t see the union’s radical potential put into action nearly enough. This is a result of it being dominated by moderate Labor students who want to stay on the good side of management. While students are increasingly squeezed by the cost of living, increasingly indebted to the university and facing a hostile world of far-right maniacs, the union has refused to put up a fight. Years of this passive, moderate leadership have led to the present situation. The university is confident it can get rid of the union because few students even know what it is.

We need to fight to defend the union, but it also needs to be rebuilt into a fighting left-wing body that students know will stand up for them. Today’s protest was the first step in what will be a long campaign to defeat the university’s attacks. Convincing students of the importance of the student union and mobilising them to fight back is the best way the union can defend itself.

author: Ben Radford
title: Racism against First Nations people is ‘like a cancer’, federal inquiry told
content:
A three-month-long federal inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people wrapped up in Naarm/Melbourne on August 7.

It received hundreds of written submissions, detailing widespread abuse, harassment and structural discrimination against First Nations people.

It was called in response to a racist attack on Camp Sovereignty, in Naarm in August last year, and an attempted terrorist attack on an Invasion Day rally in Boorloo/Perth in January.

At public hearings across the country, harrowing accounts of attacks on First Nations people were given. They included attacks on community events for Stolen Generations survivors, First Nations children being bullied for their culture and police ignoring First Nations’ survivors of domestic violence.

First Nations legal service officers told the inquiry that racism is entrenched in child protection systems, pointing to the removal of children from their families and communities to culturally unsafe environments. Today, more First Nations children are being taken from their families than at any time during the Stolen Generations; about 20,000 children live in out-of-home care across the country.

There were accounts of First Nations communities being subjected to torrents of online racism, at the Gimuy/Cairns public hearing, which the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners described as a “public health emergency”.

Ngarrindjeri woman Marissa Williamson Pohlman, the first First Nations women boxer to represent Australia at the Olympic games, told the inquiry about the widespread abuse and racism in Boxing Australia. Other sportspeople and representatives from community sporting organisations gave details about the racism First Nations players and clubs face every day.

Millions of racist posts and comments about First Nations people are often algorithmically boosted by design and by social media companies’ failure to moderate content on their platforms. Representatives from Meta — Facebook and Instagram’s parent company — revealed to the inquiry that none of its content moderators were First Nations or based in Australia.

The Northern Land Council (NLC) said in its submission that “racism, hate and violence experienced by Aboriginal people in Australia today must be understood as the direct legacy of historical processes and legal doctrines instituted through colonisation”.

The NLC said the 2023 Voice to Parliament referendum marked a “critical inflection point” and that, since then, it has observed “a clear increase in the openness and hostility of racism”.

NLC CEO Yuseph Deen told the inquiry on July 15 in Garramilla/Darwin that the impact of online racism on young First Nations people’s sense of identity and belonging is a huge concern. “That harm is real, and it is measurable,” Deen said.

The normalisation of online racism and abuse translates into real-life attacks on First Nations people, such as 56-year-old Andrew Brien deliberately running over two 12-year-old-boys with his car in Mildura, Victoria, earlier this month.

Two people again attacked Camp Sovereignty on August 2, leaving 37-year-old Ash Ni Mara, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Palawa person, with facial injuries.

Victorian independent senator Lidia Thorpe, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman, who is one of the members of the parliamentary committee leading the inquiry, said racism in Australia is “like a cancer”.

Thorpe had wanted the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion to also include racism against First Nations peoples, but she, like others, was ignored. She said the inquiry must address systemic racism and the “structural barriers embedded in systems and institutions across this country that quietly keep us down”.

Thorpe said the inquiry “must not become another tick-a-box exercise, or a delaying tactic that ends in another long report added to the too-hard basket”.

State and territory governments’ refusals to participate in the public hearings — with the exception of Tasmania — show their lack of commitment to even discuss the racism embedded in their courts, police, hospitals, schools and child protection systems.

While there is a significant under-reporting of statistics, multiple studies and reports point to growing racism against First Nations people.

Reconciliation Australia found that 54% of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people surveyed in 2024 had experienced racism in the previous six months — a …

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: Transportation in Sydney is highway robbery
content:
Sydneysiders pay, on average,

more than 15 percent of their income

 just getting around the city week-to-week. It’s a scam that hits working-class residents hardest.

On one hand, there’s the broken public transport system. According to Deutsche Bank’s

Mapping the World’s Prices

 report

, which compares prices across 69 world cities, Sydney’s public transport is the second most expensive in the world, with residents paying up to $2,600 per year in fares. On top of that, the government pays billions to private companies that provide many of the services. The Greater Sydney Bus contract is worth nearly $8 billion, while a private contractor is being paid nearly $4 billion to operate the Metro. So workers pay twice to fund this corporate gravy train—first with their Opal card and again in taxes to fund the companies that profit from running the services.

Yet while costs have soared, the services have gotten worse. Private companies, for example, operate all bus services in the metro area. But the routes are often disrupted, with reduced services and poorer pay and conditions for drivers. The buses are often crowded, if they even show up. In 2023, the ABC

revealed

 that Sydney’s bus contractors were earning bonuses by cancelling thousands of services to meet “on time” targets. “Ghost buses”—ones scheduled to arrive but never do—are common.

The city’s outer suburbs are the least well-served. A 2024

Bus Industry Taskforce report

 found that 235 bus routes failed to meet “minimum service standards”. Most of the routes are in western Sydney. The report said the government needed to invest $10 billion in the coming decades to fix the network.

It is no better for those driving their cars: Sydneysiders pay more than $1 billion in road tolls annually. The city’s thirteen major toll roads are often unavoidable. Transurban, the main company involved, is one of many corporate leeches growing fat off public assets. Many major Transurban toll roads feature locked-in annual price increases of 4 percent or the rate of inflation (whichever is higher), ensuring continuous price hikes for drivers. ​

The state Labor government introduced a $50-per-week toll cap in the latest budget, but it is inadequate. Drivers still pay up to $2,600 per year so that Transurban shareholders can enrich themselves. The cap also leaves the toll road racket untouched. Rather than ending the flow of money to Transurban, the government simply reimburses motorists after they have paid tolls out of pocket. The whole system is highway robbery.

​The first steps to solving the problems are abolishing road tolls, and bringing public transport back into public hands and making it free. Workers should not have to pay for the “privilege” of getting around our own city.

But these measures should only be the beginning. For decades, the city has been designed to make people dependent on cars. The destruction of Sydney’s extensive tram network in the 1950s was one part of this. But more cars and roads relative to trains and trams made congestion worse as the city expanded. A massive investment in public transport infrastructure is needed to reshape Sydney in the interests of working-class residents.

author: Thomas More
title: On the Concept of History & Paralipomena - Walter Benjamin
content:
Transcribed from Selected Writings. Volume 4: 1938-1940, ed. Howard Eiland (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2006), 389-411.

There was once, we know, an automaton constructed in such a way that it could respond to every move by a chess player with a countermove that would ensure the winning of the game.1 A puppet wearing Turkish attire and with a hookah in its mouth sat before a chessboard placed on a large table. A system of mirrors created the illusion that this table was transpar­ent on all sides. Actually, a hunchbacked dwarf—a master at chess—sat in­side and guided the puppet’s hand by means of strings. One can imagine a philosophic counterpart to this apparatus. The puppet, called “historical materialism,”2 is to win all the time. It can easily be a match for anyone if it enlists the services of theology, which today, as we know, is small and ugly and has to keep out of sight.

“It is one of the most noteworthy peculiarities of the human heart,” writes Lotze, “that so much selfishness in individuals coexists with the general lack of envy which every present day feels toward its future.”3 This observation indicates that the image of happiness we cherish is thoroughly colored by the time to which the course of our own existence has assigned us. There is happiness—such as could arouse envy in us—only in the air we have breathed, among people we could have talked to, women who could have given themselves to us. In other words, the idea of happiness is indissolubly bound up with the idea of redemption. The same applies to the idea of the past, which is the concern of history. The past carries with it a secret index by which it is referred to redemption. Doesn’t a breath of the air that per­vaded earlier days caress us as well? In the voices we hear, isn’t there an echo of now silent ones? Don’t the women we court have sisters they no longer recognize? If so, then there is a secret agreement between past gener­ations and the present one. Then our coming was expected on earth. Then, like every generation that preceded us, we have been endowed with a weak messianic power, a power on which the past has a claim. Such a claim can­not be settled cheaply. The historical materialist is aware of this.

The chronicler who narrates events without distinguishing between major and minor ones acts in accord with the following truth: nothing that has ever happened should be regarded as lost to history. pf course only a re­deemed mankind is granted the fullness of its past—which is to say, only for a redeemed mankind has its past become citable in all its moments. Each moment it has lived becomes a citation à l’ordre du jour.4 And that day is Judgment Day.

Seek for food and clothing first; then shall the Kingdom of God be granted to you. —Hegel, 18075

Class struggle, which for a historian schooled in Marx is always in evi­dence, is a fight for the crude and material things without which no refined and spiritual things could exist. But these latter things, which are present in class struggle, are not present as a vision of spoils that fall to the victor. They are alive in this struggle as confidence, courage, humor, cunning, and fortitude, and have effects that reach far back into the past. They constantly call into question every victory, past and present, of the rulers. As flowers turn toward the sun, what has been strives to turn—by dint of a secret heliotropism—toward that sun which is rising in the sky of history. The his­torical materialist must be aware of this most inconspicuous of all transfor­mations.

The true image of the past flits by. The past can be seized only as an image that flashes up at the moment of its recognizability, and is never seen again. “The truth will not run away from us”: this statement by Gottfried Keller indicates exactly that point in historicism’s image of history where the im­age is pierced by historical materialism.6 For it is an irretrievable image of the past which threatens to disappear in any present that does not recognize itself as intended in that image.

Articulating the past historically does not mean recognizing it “the way it really was.”7 It means appropriating a memory as it flashes up in a moment of danger. Historical materialism wishes to hold fast that image of the past which unexpectedly appears to the historical subject in a moment of danger. The danger threatens both the content of the tradition and those who in­herit it. For both, it is one and the same thing: the …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Israeli Commander “Not Sorry” for Ordering WCK Strike That Killed 7 Aid Workers
content:
Rights groups said it was a likely war crime that helped build evidence for Israel’s practice of using starvation as a weapon in Gaza.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The Israeli commander who ordered the strike on World Central Kitchen (WCK) aid workers in Gaza in 2024 said that he has no regrets for the incident that sparked global outrage and worsened famine conditions in the Strip.

Nochi Mendel, a colonel who was dismissed from his position as the chief of staff of the Nahal infantry brigade, told Australian public broadcaster ABC that he believes that the strike was justified, even though rights groups said it was a likely war crime that helped build evidence for Israel’s practice of using starvation as a weapon in Gaza.

“I’m the commander, and I’m the one who gave the order to carry out the operation,” said Mendel, through a translator. “I’m not sorry for what I did.”

The strike killed seven aid workers: Palestinian driver Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha; British nationals John Chapman, James Henderson, and James Kirby; Canadian-American Jacob Flickinger; Zomi Frankcom, an Australian; and Damian Soból, from Poland. It sparked international condemnation, highlighting Israel’s practice of targeting aid workers. As of April 2026, Israel had killed 560 aid workers in Gaza amid the genocide.

After the strike, the Israeli military said that it was “conducting a thorough review at the highest levels to understand the circumstances of this tragic incident.” Mendel and another commander on the brigade were dismissed for “violation” of procedures.

However, last week, the military announced that it was not doing a criminal probe into the commanders responsible for the incident, sparking renewed outrage.

“At the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” WCK said in response to the decision. “It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”

Mendel, recounting the incident to ABC, claimed that he didn’t intend to kill the WCK workers, even though he’s not apologetic about the outcome. He said that the attack was justified because he found out after the strike that WCK had links to Hamas — allegations WCK said were “false and outrageous.”

“This is the latest attempt to shift blame away from the IDF’s own actions,” a WCK spokesperson said. “The individual making these slanderous claims has no credibility.”

Indeed, even in his own accounting, Mendel seems to subtly admit that he purposefully killed WCK workers.

Mendel says that he was watching the convoy move through a drone, while he was at a control center in Israel’s Sde Teiman military facility. He said that he saw gunmen moving with the convoy — which the Israeli military later identified as security hired by WCK — which he said were “terrorists,” who were moving alongside aid workers in the vehicles.

He said that, after the convoy stopped at a warehouse and got back on its way, he saw a person with a gun enter a car, which he described as an “armed terrorist.” Mendel says that the people operating from the drone base “definitely confirm that they identified an armed terrorist in the vehicle” — so he ordered the strike.

The gun that Mendel claims he saw the person carrying turned out to be a bag. Having watched the aid workers reload at the warehouse, Mendel would have known that the vehicles in the convoy had aid workers in them. And the vehicle had a clear and large WCK logo adhered to its roof, in clear view of a drone.

Pro-Israel figures have claimed that the strike did not violate international law because Mendel could have believed he was targeting fighters. But international law dictates that militaries must not strike civilians, and that they should refrain from attacking if there is a possibility of civilian casualties.

Mendel says now that “maybe one” or no combatants were killed in the strike. No evidence has shown that the aid workers were involved with Hamas’s militant wing.

Mendel said that his main disappointment is that he was dismissed by the Israeli military after the strike.

“It’s a matter of it being painful because you’re fighting a very complex situation,” he said. “In the end, in a very difficult situation, I’m paying …

author: Ellen Cassedy
title: Dolly Parton Helped Us to Speak Up and Join Together
content:
Dolly Parton’s song, “9 to 5,” has endured as a beloved anthem for nearly half a century.  What many people don’t know is that the direct inspiration for the song—and the hit movie—was the 9 to 5 working women’s movement that began in Boston in the early 1970’s.  It was the movement that inspired the song and the movie—and the song and the movie gave the movement a giant boost.


In 1972, I was one of ten women office workers who started sitting in a circle on our lunch hour talking about our jobs.  We talked about low pay.  Unequal pay.  Training men to be our own supervisors.  Having to do favors—all kinds of favors— for our bosses.


Before long, our group became a significant factor in Boston’s labor scene.  Wielding media coverage, government pressure, and creative demonstrations of office workers’ discontent, we won millions of dollars in back pay and raises and improved women’s job situation throughout the city.  After a few years we went national, with chapters from coast to coast, and our woman-led union, District 925 of the Service Employees (SEIU), began to take shape.


Enter Jane Fonda.  Jane knew one of our leaders, Karen Nussbaum, from the antiwar movement, and when she said she’d decided to make a movie about the concerns of office workers, we were over the moon.  She met with our members to plumb their frustrations, revenge fantasies, and aspirations.  And in a stroke of genius, she invited Dolly to join the cast.


Dolly was already a superstar as a singer and songwriter, but she’d never been in a film.  Alongside Jane and comedian Lily Tomlin, she turned out to be a natural in her role as Doralee Rhodes, the sweet and greatly annoyed target of lecherous attention from her evil boss.


One day on the set she took out her guitar.  “I’ve got a song,” she said.


Her toe-tapping tune perfectly encapsulated working women’s grievances and our dreams.  It begins with pride, moves on to anger, then summons a sense of collective purpose.  It ends with victory: “The tide’s gonna turn, and it’s all gonna roll your way!”


Before 9 to 5, office workers had never been the main characters on the big screen.  In fact, although we were 20 million strong—one third of America’s female workforce—we were basically invisible.  When people pictured a worker, they saw a man in a hard hat brandishing a wrench.  But now audiences were laughing and cheering as the three women managed to remove their boss from the office and implement a slew of worker-friendly policies, from job-sharing to flex-time to child care.


The film made clear that the problem was the boss, not the secretaries, and that the answer was women taking collective action.  As people howled at the boss’s ridiculous antics, they realized that the old ways had to go.  The American office was never the same.


One morning shortly after the movie came out when I was riding the bus to work, I overheard one woman talking to another. “So I said to him,” she said, “‘No, I will not make your coffee!’ I just saw 9 to 5!”


Dolly’s way of contributing to that sea-change was all her own.


While Jane Fonda headlined our public events and spoke eloquently to the media about our issues, Dolly did not.  She walked no picket lines and made no public statements. Instead, she served as a powerful model.  She knew working women, knew the obstacles to success from the inside.  Her warmth and empathy were boundless.  Just by being who she was, she helped forge a path for countless women, helping them to move forward from silence to making common cause with coworkers.


In 2019, the podcaster Jad Abumrad asked Dolly if she thought of herself as a feminist.  “No, I do not,” she responded.  “I think of myself as a woman in business.”


Later she spoke a bit differently to

Time

 magazine.  "I suppose I am a feminist,” she said, “if I believe that women should be able to do anything they want to."


Such statements were typical of many of the women who joined 9 to 5.  They didn’t see themselves as part of the women’s liberation movement, yet they believed passionately in fairness and equality on the job.  Our movement worked hard to provide a safe space for such women, along with those who did feel comfortable with the feminist label.  Dolly’s example and her outsized presence helped us create that safe space and build unity among women all along the political spectrum.


Decade after decade, Dolly helped us to speak up and join together.  We owe her a debt.


[Ellen Cassedy was …

author: Shane Burley
title: The movement to defend the Minneapolis 15
content:
This article

The movement to defend the Minneapolis 15

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


When Minneapolis organizer Alec Stewart pulled out of his parking spot on June 16 and headed to work, it seemed like an ordinary day. That is, until Homeland Security Investigations, a detective-like sub-agency of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, rolled up with multiple squad cars and dragged him out of his vehicle. 


“I was never told I was arrested,” said Stewart, who goes by Mac. “I was not told what for. I was not shown any warrants. I had no idea [I was going to be arrested] until I was in cuffs.”


Mac was among the thousands of Minnesotans who rallied to defend their neighbors this January when Trump inundated Minneapolis-St. Paul with federal immigration agents who outnumbered regular police 3 to 1. Residents responded with one of the

most sweeping, complex and powerful movements of the decade

, mobilizing a multitude of existing relationships and organizations to craft a shield capable of fighting off Trump’s domestic militia. Using the encrypted app Signal, they built networks to track officers and warn potential arrestees. They launched mutual aid networks to support those who were in hiding to avoid becoming targets of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. They blockaded roads, tailed ICE vehicles and went out on a one-day general strike. 


The charges faced by Mac and his 14 co-defendants, all of whom were arrested on the same day, carry multi-year sentences. The government claims all 15 people indicted “did knowingly conspire … to prevent by force, intimidation and threats, officers and employees of the United States Department of Homeland Security … from discharging the duties of their officers,” while individual defendants have been charged with additional crimes like assault on a federal officer. The alleged “conspiracy” involved everything from conversations in Signal chats about plans to blockade an ICE processing center, to assigning working groups for the Jan. 23 General Strike, to possessing homemade defensive shields or just following federal officers — as tens of thousands around the country have done. 


What’s particularly alarming to the defendants and their allies is that the charges don’t cite any specific officers who were assaulted, and the government’s evidence includes mundane activist chatter: discussing protests and ICE locations, posting an article from the anarchist website CrimethInc. Anything provably tied to organizing, or just radical ideas, became proof of conspiracy: renting a U-Haul, purchasing a trailer from Facebook Marketplace, calling on Facebook for the public to “become ungovernable” — all were alleged evidence of malicious intent. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


What’s also alarming is how that information was gathered. Recently, the defense filed a motion that revealed the existence of Operation Puppet Master, a

program to surveil and investigate

 Twin Cities labor unions, churches and community groups in advance of the filing of criminal charges. author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Canadian North flight attendants file for third-party mediation
content:
Close to 200 flight attendants at Canadian North have filed a notice of dispute, saying there has been a lack of meaningful progress since contract negotiations with the airline began in March.


Salary, unpaid hours, working conditions and scheduling are among the top sticking points at the bargaining table, said a news release from CUPE  8111, the chapter of the Canadian Union of Public Employees that represents the workers.


“Our members are struggling,” union president Isabelle Paquette wrote in the release.


The union’s decision to file a notice of dispute triggers a conciliation process under federal labour law, which means a third party appointed by the government will intervene to help both sides reach an agreement within 60 days. That deadline can be extended with the consent of both parties.


It’s also a necessary first step before a union can strike or before a lockout can occur.


Wages have not kept up with the cost of living, Paquette said in the news release.


“Flight attendants are essential to the North,” she said. “Our members work hard to keep northern communities connected, and they deserve fair compensation for the work they do.”


Nunatsiaq News has reached out to the union for an interview but did not receive a response by press time.


Canadian North operates flights across Nunavut and the N.W.T. and connects northern communities to southern cities.


Canadian North is “committed to respectful, good-faith collective bargaining” and “welcomes the opportunity to continue negotiations through the conciliation process,” c

ompany spokesperson Hance Colburne wrote in an email to Nunatsiaq News.


Colburne said the airline isn’t anticipating any disruption to its operations.


He didn’t provide details about what Canadian North currently offers workers, saying only that the airline must recognize “the needs of our employees and customers while supporting the long-term sustainability of our airline.”

Despite being branded as autonomous and self-sustaining, artificial intelligence relies heavily on human labor — an army of data workers all over the world, primarily in the Global South. These workers “are purposely hidden by the companies that produce AI because they are the secret ingredient of AI itself,” says sociologist Antonio Casilli, the author of Waiting for Robots: The Hired Hands of Automation and co-writer of the documentary In the Belly of AI. Casilli estimates that over 160 million people are involved in data work around the world.

One of the most discussed aspects of how artificial intelligence will transform society is how it will impact jobs and labor. On Wednesday, Bill Gates published a nearly 6,000-word essay in which he warned that society is not ready for the transformation and upheaval AI will cause. In the essay, Gates calls AI’s impact on the labor force one of the three primary risks of the technology, saying many jobs will disappear forever and that, quote, “AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice.”

But what gets much less discussion is how artificial intelligence has already transformed work globally. Le mercredi 26 août,

 le pouvoir exécutif du gouvernement américain a sanctionné Autistici/Inventati,

un petit fournisseur Internet italien militant et géré par des bénévoles,

 pour avoir prétendument fourni des services à des organisations terroristes (voir

le communiqué de presse du Département d'État

).


May First condamne catégoriquement cette désignation et

Cette désignation est familière à May First –

c'est la même méthode utilisée contre

l'ancien membre de May First, Samidoun

. Comme nous l'avons noté dans notre courrier électronique de l'année dernière, le gouvernement américain peut effectivement isoler n'importe quelle organisation

sans présenter de preuves ni de procès

 en alléguant simplement qu'elle soutient le terrorisme.


Lorsqu'une organisation est inscrite sur la liste des

ressortissants spécialement désignés (SDN)

, il devient illégal pour toute personne ou organisation américaine de lui fournir des services ou de collaborer avec elle de quelque manière que ce soit.

Cela peut signifier perdre l'accès aux comptes bancaires, aux services financiers, la possibilité de recevoir des dons et tout autre service

autistici.org

Qu'est-ce qu'Autistici/Inventati ?


Nous encourageons tout le monde à lire la

Défendre la technologie du mouvement indépendant


Autistici, comme May First, est un petit fournisseur d'accès Internet autonome doté d'une infime fraction des ressources des grandes entreprises technologiques. Les cibler de sanctions américaines est excessif et vindicatif :

title: Zur Zukunft der Anstadt - Anstadt Bleibt! 29.08.2026
content:
An alle Solidarischen, alle Interessierten, an die Öffentlichkeit und an die Politik.


Aktuelles Kassenfurz Video zum Thema:

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/iPYTMmnsAVs


Sommer 2026: Es ist heiss und trocken – auch in Bern. Im Schatten der hohen Bäume, am


südlichsten Zipfel des Gaswerkareals, besteht die Anstadt bereits im neunten Sommer. Rund um die Überbauungspläne der Stadt ist es seit der Abstimmung im November letzten Jahres wiederruhig geworden. Im Hintergrund läuft ein Eingabe-Wettbewerb für diejenigen konkurrierenden Genossenschaften, welche sich für ein Stückchen Land vom Anstadt-Kuchen bewerben. Die gut ein Hektar grosse Fläche soll dabei gedrittelt und im Baurecht verkauft werden.

Die Anstadt soll ganz selbstverständlich verdrängt werden, was sowohl in der Politik wie auch bei den Genossenschaften nur die Wenigsten zu kümmern scheint.

 Das soll sich jetzt ändern:


Die Anstadt bleibt!


So lautet die Zukunftsdevise der Kollektive, die auf dem Flecken Erde der Anstadt ihre


Existenzgrundlage aufgebaut haben. Wir finden, ein Ort, an dem so viele Menschen, Projekte und Veranstaltungen zusammenkommen und der gleichzeitig der Natur wertvollen Lebensraum bietet, muss erhalten und verteidigt werden.

Die Anstadt verstand sich noch nie als Zwischennutzung. Sie ist durch eine Land-Besetzung entstanden.

 Auch wenn die Behörden später einen Zwischennutzungsvertrag verlangt haben, heisst das nicht, dass die Anstadt nur einen temporären Anspruch auf Freiraum stellt.


Die Hitze in diesem Sommer hat es gezeigt: Die verbleibenden Grünflächen im Herzen der Stadt


abzuholzen und mit Beton zu versiegeln ist akuter Unsinn!

Baut auf dem Teil des Gaswerkareals, wo seit Jahren nichts als Staub und Trockenheit besteht, aber fasst die Bäume und das unkommerzielle Freiraumprojekt nicht an!

 Selbst aus baulicher Sicht ist das Areal der Anstadt eine absolut ungeeignete Fläche, um grosse Blocks hinzubauen: Das Grundwasser drückt bei Starkregen bis an die Oberfläche. Zudem ist der Boden laut neusten Untersuchungen der Firma

Geotest

 anscheinend erheblich belastet, was das Bauen zusätzlich verteuern würde und bei notwendigen Sanierungsarbeiten womöglich sogar das Grundwasser verschmutzen könnte.

Die Ergebnisse der Bodenproben sind darum Gegenstand öffentlichen Interessens, und müssen baldmöglichst veröffentlicht werden!


Natur und Mensch findet mit der Anstadt eine rare und dringend-notwendige lebendig-grüne Insel. Viele Menschen, einige davon strukturell benachteiligt und unterdrückt, haben sich hier ihr Zuhause aufgebaut. Wir haben viel Zeit und Energie investiert, um ein basisdemokratisches Zusammenleben zu ermöglichen und sich damit dem profitorientierten Immobilienmarkt zu widersetzen. Wann immer Orte, an denen eine andere Gesellschaftsform erprobt wird, nach Jahren einer friedlichen Existenz, zerstört werden, entsteht eine Kluft, die Verbundenheit auftrennt und Frust generiert.

Wenn die Anstadt sterben sollte, dann werden Menschen verdrängt, dann wird gegenseitige Unterstützung erschwert und die Möglichkeit Utopie zu Realität werden zu lassen, erstickt.


Baut, aber nicht hier!


Es ist frustrierend, dass keine Fragen über die Zukunft der Anstadt gestellt werden: Die


Stadtregierung ist noch nie auf die Anstadt zugekommen. Die Planungsbehörde löscht die Anstadt sogar kurzerhand aus jedem Portfolio und Luftbild, als würde sie nicht existieren. Gemeinsam verkaufen sie öffentlichen Grund im Baurecht, um kurzfristig Natur zu zerstören und längerfristig einen Tropfen Wohnen auf den heissen Stein zu vergiessen. Ein Leben in der

Stadt kann es längerfristig nur für alle geben, wenn das Privateigentum hinterfragt wird.


Wir fordern:


• Eine sofortige Unterbrechung der Baufelder-Ausschreibung für den Sektor 1.5 (Anstadt), bis


der Bericht zur Bodenbelastung veröffentlicht ist.


• Wir wünschen uns die solidarische Nicht-Bewerbung von Genossenschaften auf Baufelder


in der Anstadt.


• Ein Eingehen der Stadt auf die Anliegen der Anstadt und der Natur.


• Den Miteinbezug der Anstadt in die Überbauungspläne des Gaswerkareals und damit eine


zukunftsfähige Lösung für alle Beteiligten.


Wir rufen alle betroffenen Menschen dazu auf, sich an der Diskussion zu beteiligen, um die


Stadt Bern von unten zu gestalten.


Es grüsst,
