title: Deniz Göktaş'ın avukatları: "Kişiyi ne olursa olsun cezaevinde tutma" anlayışı diriliyor
content:
Komedyen Deniz Göktaş’ın avukatları, müvekkillerinin tahliye kararının hemen sonrasında tekrar tutuklanmasıyla ilgili bir açıklama yayımladı. 


İtiraz kabul edilerek Göktaş için tahliye kararı verildi


"Kamuoyuna" hitaben yayımlanan açıklamada, Ceza Muhakemesi Kanunu'nun (CMK) 108. Maddesi uyarınca, otuz günde bir Deniz Göktaş'ın tutukluluk incelemesi yapıldığını; 24 Ağustos'ta gerçekleştirilen son tutukluluk incelemesinde tutukluluk hâlinin devamına karar verildiğini; ancak yapılan itirazın 28 Ağustos saat 17.03 itibarıyla İstanbul Nöbetçi Asliye Ceza Mahkemesince kabul edildiğini ve Göktaş'ın tutuklu bulunduğu "Cumhurbaşkanına Hakaret" ve "Halkı Kin ve Düşmanlığa Tahrik" suçlarından  tahliyesine karar verildiği belirtildi.  


Tahliye müzekkeresi yazılmadan yeniden tutuklama istendi


Bu karardan sonraki gelişmeleri avukatlar şöyle özetledi: 


"Üzülerek ifade edelim ki, daha bu karara ilişkin olarak cezaevine tahliye müzekkeresi  yazılmadan,  müvekkilimiz  “Ölü Deniz” adlı stand-up gösterisinde Daltonlar çetesini övdüğü iddiasıyla “Suçu ve Suçluyu Övme” suçunu işlediği gerekçesiyle tutuklama talebiyle İstanbul 4. Sulh Ceza Hakimliği’ne (ilk tutuklama kararı da bu hakimlik tarafından verilmiştir) sevk edilmiş, bu işlemler hakkında tarafımıza haber verilmeden Baro'dan bir avukat tayin edilmiş ve sonuç olarak müvekkilimiz tahliye edilmeden yeniden tutuklanmıştır."


Savcılık, tutuklama için mesai saati sonrası çalıştı 


Avukatlar açıklamalarının devamında savcılığın tahliye kararının heme sonrasında savcının mesai saatleri dışında çalışarak Göktaş'ı içeride tutma saikiyle suçlama yarattığını ileri sürdü: 


Savcılığın ikinci ayını tamamlayan soruşturmada, bu yeni suçlamayı tahliye kararından dakikalar sonra ve mesai saatleri dışında devreye sokması, 1970’li yıllarda ve 12 Eylül döneminde vücut bulan “Kişiyi ne olursa olsun cezaevinde tutma” anlayışının dirildiği kuşkusunu yaratmaktadır. 


Göktaş'ın avukatları, açıklamalarının sonunda, tüm itiraz haklarını sonuna kadar kullanacaklarını ve "adaletin tecelli etmesi maksadıyla hukukun sınırları içinde azami mücadeleyi yapmaya devam edece[klerini]" dile getirdiler.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Nitjautik Music Festival returns to Tasiujaq for 5th year
content:
Tasiujaq is getting ready for the fifth edition of the Nitjautik Music Festival after logistical challenges forced the event’s cancellation last year.


Crew members Liam Callaghan (top) and Ken Fraser set up the stage Thursday ahead of the fifth annual Nitjautik Music Festival in Tasiujaq. (Photo by Dominique Gené)


The festival runs Friday and Saturday at the community’s multi-use centre and will feature performers from across Nunavik and beyond.


But before the music starts, much of the work happens behind the scenes.


Peter Nassak, one of the featured performers, arrived from Kuujjuaq Wednesday to help setup.


“When I get the chance, I help out wherever I can,” he said.


Nassak, 37, has been playing music since he was a teenager and learned much of the technical side of live performance on the job.


For him, music became more than a creative pursuit.


“I wasn’t very good at regulating my emotions as a teenager,” he said. “But with music, I think it was really an escape from everything for me and that really helped.”


Nassak sings in Inuktitut and English. His music draws primarily from blues and rock. He also sees a connection between music and nature.


“If you go out into nature and you sit still, it might sound like there is nothing. But if you really listen, there are sounds everywhere.”


For his second time performing at the festival, Nassak hopes to bring people together.


“To see people smile and to connect with them, is for me the most rewarding thing when I perform,” he said.


Also among the setup crew was Liam Callaghan, who has been involved with the festival since the start, when it was a much smaller outdoor event.


“We set it up outside, with beautiful hills as a background,” Callaghan said of the inaugural festival.


In those early days, the festival had fewer resources and basic equipment.


“It was a struggle, but it was fun,” he said.


Now, the festival has grown into a two-day event. Putting it together in a remote community, though, still presents challenges.


Equipment has to arrive by boat and plane, with some supplies borrowed from nearby communities. Callaghan came to Tasiujaq in July to assess what was available and what still needed to be brought in.


At the same time, he said, the community’s willingness to pitch in makes the work easier.


“If you have to put up the curtain, say, someone will volunteer and build a frame for the curtain, and everyone just wants to help out,” he said.


Callaghan also brought in Ken Fraser, a veteran of northern festivals who has worked with Aqpik Jam in Kuujjuaq since 1996. He also worked with Eastern Arctic Summer Festival in Kuujjuarapik in 1991.


Despite his decades of experience, Fraser said he continues to learn from younger technicians.


“These young guys now are teaching me more than I could ever,” he said.


This year’s lineup includes the Trade Offs, Yaa, Kathy Snowball and others.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: CAQ ignore FNs in election promise to double resource revenue sharing: Lac Simon
content:
Quebec’s campaign for its upcoming provincial election officially began yesterday, but already the sitting Coalition Avenir du Québec (CAQ) government has found itself at odds with the Anishnabe Council of Lac Simon over a plan to increase natural resource development revenue sharing.


On Aug. 24, three days before the formal launch of the election campaign, CAQ Natural Resources Minister Kateri Champagne Jourdain announced her party would double the revenue sharing budget for natural resources from $38 million to $76 million beginning in the spring of 2027. Jourdain said the goal of the funding change was to better compensate regions of Quebec that are centres of natural resource development.


In a press release published yesterday, the

 Council of Lac Simon

 responded that they “strongly condemn[ed] the complete absence of First Nations in the election pledge made on August 24 by the Coalition Avenir Québec to increase funding for resource regions.”


First Nations, the council argued in the release, were “invisibilized” by the announcement, an omission Lac Simon’s council called “neither trivial nor acceptable.”


“First Nations are not mere observers of natural resource development in Quebec,” Lac Simon argued in the release. “They are the first to be affected by projects that transform their territories, impact their living environments, alter their landscapes and shape the future of their communities. Yet whenever the time comes to discuss the sharing of the economic benefits generated by these resources, they seem to disappear from the government’s priorities.”


As a result, the council said it was issuing a call to all of Quebec’s political parties to acknowledge that First Nations voters and Indigenous communities have a right to know “the concrete commitments the parties intend to make regarding reconciliation, economic development, the sharing of benefits, the protection of territory and respect for the rights of Indigenous peoples.”


Rather than being called to the table only when a dispute arises, the council said, First Nations should be full partners in Quebec’s economic future.


Speaking to APTN News, Lac Simon’s Chief Lucien Wabanonik said in French that the relationship between the province and First Nations is crucial to the future of Quebec.


“The issue of territorial rights cannot be ignored by any party, nor will the future government of Quebec be able to avoid or ignore it,” Wabanonik said.


“It’s going to be something that affects all resource extraction. And without First Nations and their consent, it’s going to be very difficult for any development or access to the territory. It’s going to be, more and more, an assertion of our peoples, of our nations — and that’s going to be an issue for Quebec when it comes to discussing development.”


Wabanonik said his community has struggled in dealings with the CAQ over the eight years since the party was first elected to two consecutive majority governments.


“We’ve tried to negotiate in good faith,” he said. “We’ve tried to find solutions that respect our rights and our families. Families are important because they’re the ones who hold the rights. It’s not Quebec or Canada: our territorial rights predate even the existence of the Canadian Confederation. So, what this means is that from now on, we’re going to assert ourselves more and more. Going to court will be the only option left to us, and that could have a direct impact on access to the territory.”


Read more:


Lac Simon requests judicial review of $40 million Ottawa-Quebec caribou deal


Opposition grows to proposed forestry bill in Quebec


According to Wabononik, provincial governments are in the habit of claiming they cannot reach an agreement with First Nations without a treaty. But Wabononik maintains treaties are not necessary to a healthy working relationship between Quebec and First Nations, provided governments are willing to meet the conditions First Nations set for themselves, and willing to treat families and the land with respect.


“Our rights are always recognized by the Supreme Court,” he said. “We need to reach an agreement, and we’ll negotiate in good faith and collectively. I think there are some interesting possibilities to explore. It’s not us, the First Nations, who are closing that door.”


At the same time, Wabanonik was quick to stress — as Lac Simon’s council did in its press release — that his community was not criticizing municipalities and regions …

author: Randi Beers
title: Montreal circus camp for Inuit youth flies high with public performance
content:
A young group of Inuit in Montreal are ready to fly.


They are

planning to take the stage Friday evening at the

newly built

 Sanaaq Centre for an hour-long circus performance that includes

flying trapeze, Inuit drumming and Inuit games, all set to music by musicians such as Elisapie.


The performance is a culmination of what the group learned this summer during a two-week circus camp called Nikurrautaq, led by Tupiq Arctic Circus Troupe.


The camp, led by a group of Inuit circus performers who come from Kativik Regional Government’s Cirqiniq program, is aimed at urban Inuit between the ages of 12 and 17 years old. 


“It came simply out of desire to transmit our knowledge and skills to Inuit youth that live here,” said Saali Kuata, a co-ordinator of the camp.


“These children crave more,” he added. “Trying to respond to that, we look within ourselves, to make ourselves available, and find the right spaces.”


This is the second rendition of the camp.


Last year, as a pilot project, most of the activities were hosted outside, and the camp only lasted a few days. This year the troupe upgraded its curriculum by hosting activities at the Verdun Circus School and the Sanaaq Centre’s 255-seat performance hall. 


Changing to an official performance venue makes a difference for the kids, said Kuata.


“Coming to a space like this really ties the whole thing together,” he said, pointing to production capabilities like lights and music. “It is going to be a lasting memory for them, it is really a privilege.”


To start a program like this is no easy task, Kuata said. He and his team were taught by senior instructors with decades of experience.


Now, “we are going into that foray of becoming the facilitators, becoming the animators, becoming the scheduler,” he said.


For Kuata, the circus teaches youth important lessons about confidence and self-expression.


“Like exposure therapy, it is forcing ourselves to be embarrassed or to fail,” he said.

“[We want] to continue fostering these skills and abilities that they are going to carry for the rest of their lives.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Jordin Tootoo, Attima Hadlari to be inducted into Nunavut sport hall of fame
content:
After months of planning, the Nunavut Sport Federation is launching its new Nunavut Sport and

Recreation Hall of Fame, with a ceremony planned in Iqaluit this fall.


The late Attima Hadlari drum-dances at the Kitikmeot Inuit Association’s community feast in Cambridge Bay in 2017. (File photo by Jane George)


The two inaugural

inductees will be former NHL right winger

Jordin Tootoo

, from Rankin Inlet, and late Inuit games athlete

Attima Hadlari

.


“We have a virtual hall of fame set up,” said federation operations manager Scott Schultz Friday in an email. “

Moving forward we are hoping to have a physical hall of fame, but we have not found a space yet.”


The hall of fame could eventually be spread across Nunavut’s three regions, he added, with the Kivalliq, Kitikmeot and Qikiqtaaluk each getting their own installation.


From 2003 to 2017, Tootoo, played 723 games for the Nashville Predators, Detroit Red Wings, New Jersey Devils and Chicago Blackhawks.

He racked up 65 goals, 96 assists and 1,010 penalty minutes during that time.


Hadlari was an Arctic sports athlete from Cambridge Bay

who mastered the sealskin whip and went on to coach and officiate for young athletes participating in traditional Inuit games.


He also served in the first Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit Katimajiit, which gives expertise in how to apply Inuit traditional knowledge in government, from 2003 to 2005.


The pair are scheduled to be inducted during the

 Sport and Recreation Awards Gala at Aqsarniit Hotel on Oct. 3.


The federation,

a non-profit that supports the territory’s sport organizations,

 is working with Tootoo and both inductees’ families to try to have them in attendance at the gala, Schultz said.

title: Kalkan: Everyone should approach the process with sensitivity
content:
Duran Kalkan, a member of the Abdullah Öcalan Social Sciences Academy, made important assessments of current developments during a special program broadcast on Medya Haber television.


We publish excerpts of the interview. 


The Follow-up and Evaluation Commission held its first meeting. This was seen as an important development, but we also see that there have been provocations, and Leader Apo has also made assessments on this issue recently.


First of all, I respectfully salute Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan]. Yes, today Leader Apo made a statement regarding the process, and the President of Turkey also made assessments and expressed views on the process in clearer and more definitive terms. What we see is that the parties are more determined and clearer in advancing the process. This was clearly expressed both in the statement from the Turkish Presidency and in Leader Apo’s statement. That is certain, first of all. Of course, an important aspect of the statements was that they contained a warning in the face of the provocative attempts of those opposed to the process. They made clear that no provocation could constitute an obstacle to the development of the process and that the Peace and Democratic Society Process would be successfully carried forward and advanced. This is quite important and clear.


This also shows that there are attacks coming from many fronts. In particular, there is opposition to the process from rent-seeking circles, racist circles, and, how shall I put it, some very arrogant and delusional circles. But some racist and rent-seeking circles have become much more aggressive recently.


They are attempting to sabotage the process by staging various fabricated schemes, wondering whether they might somehow derail it. Of course, this has existed from the beginning. But it appears to have increased somewhat recently. What does this indicate? It means there is development in the process, there is progress, and there is greater determination. If this were not the case, if the process were not moving forward and there was no progress, there would obviously be no need for so many attacks. There would not be such multifaceted attacks coming from so many fronts. The existence of these provocations clearly demonstrates the progress being made in the process.


In short, the process is moving forward, and it has accelerated recently. We know that with the law referred to as the framework law, which passed parliament on the night of August 10, the process actually entered its second phase as well—the phase of developing its legal and political dimensions. For the first time, a legal step was taken. Of course, many democratic circles responded to it with criticism. The Kurdish side also criticized its shortcomings, mistakes, narrow scope, lack of inclusiveness, and language. But at the same time, it strongly embraced its historical significance and importance.


This was Leader Apo’s position from the outset. He assessed that the law had at least temporarily stopped the war and opened the way for the parties to engage in politics, creating an opportunity to do so. He considered this highly important. Freeing a century-old, grave problem such as democratization and the Kurdish question—a whole complex of problems shaped entirely around violence—from this framework, opening the way for politics in these matters, and making it possible to seek solutions to problems through political means is no simple matter. Leader Apo described this as moving “from the gallows to the table.” The situation was that important and serious, both in terms of the Kurdish question and democratization. Of course, shortcomings can be criticized; that is a separate matter. But its historical significance was on this level.


Within this framework, new steps are also being taken. The body responsible for carrying out the process outlined by the law held its first meeting as of August 24. This is another important step.


Our basic criteria


It is clear that there is determination. There has also been some acceleration, particularly on the part of the state and government, which are now taking steps more quickly. The public has been informed that four subcommissions have been established, and their members have been named. What is their framework? Who will they consist of? How will they work? These things are not clear and have not been sufficiently explained to the public. They will undoubtedly be explained in due course, and we hope …

title: FEDA takes over Freedom Vigil for Abdullah Öcalan
content:
The Democratic Alevi Federation in Europe (FEDA), based in France, has taken over the Freedom Vigil in Strasbourg, home to the institutions of the Council of Europe, in its 739th week.


The vigil, which has continued uninterrupted since June 2012, has been maintained since Sunday by FEDA Co-chair Şahin Polat and FEDA members Daimi Gören, Eylem Çiçek, Veli Tekiner and Sidar Içli.


 


FEDA Co-chair Şahin Polat said on behalf of the group that the vigil represents an ongoing struggle against the stance of European states on the Kurdish question following Abdullah Öcalan’s handover to Turkey in 1999.


Polat said FEDA members had volunteered to take part in the vigil and regarded supporting the action as a responsibility, particularly at a time when efforts are underway to implement Abdullah Öcalan’s “Call for Peace and a Democratic Society.”


We see peace as a responsibility we must fulfil


Polat stressed the importance of the struggle for peace for Alevis and said: “Just as deeply as we mourn the lives we have lost, those who have fallen, we see working for peace as a responsibility we must fulfil.”


Polat said they had taken over the vigil for one week to support Abdullah Öcalan’s call. He added: “We are here to respond to Mr. Öcalan’s call for peace, conscious that we Alevis will be among those who benefit most from peace. We are here to once again lend our voice and support to the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society, and to demand Mr. Öcalan’s freedom and his right to hope.”


Polat said, “We are actors for peace and a safeguard of democratic society, and we stand behind Mr. Öcalan’s call for peace.”


FEDA Co-chair Polat also reiterated from Strasbourg the demand for the freedom of all political prisoners, alongside Abdullah Öcalan.

title: Mass graves must be opened
content:
As discussions continue over ending the conflict in Turkey and launching a new peace process, the fate of thousands of people who have been missing for years is once again coming to the fore. Although the Kurdish Freedom Movement has released the names of some guerrillas who lost their lives in clashes, the whereabouts and burial places of many of their remains are still unknown.


Since the 1990s in particular, families of the missing have struggled to recover the remains of their relatives and have them identified. The Saturday Mothers/People have also continued their longstanding protests, demanding that the fate of the missing be disclosed and that families be able to recover their loved ones.


According to data from the Human Rights Association (IHD), the remains of 4,201 people are believed to be buried in 348 identified mass graves across Turkey, some of which have been excavated while others remain unopened. Families and human rights organisations are calling for mass graves to be excavated in accordance with scientific standards, for identification procedures to be accelerated, and for the remains of those who disappeared during the years of conflict to be returned to their families.


According to IHD reports, the provinces with the highest concentration of mass graves include Diyarbakır (Amed), Siirt (Sêrt), Bitlis (Bedlîs), Şırnak (Şirnex), Van (Wan), Hakkari (Colemêrg) and Bingöl (Çewlîg). These areas have been among those most severely affected by the conflict since the 1990s.


The issue is not confined to the past. The Kurdish Freedom Movement has recently released the names of a number of guerrillas who lost their lives in clashes. However, families are reportedly still unaware of where many of those named were buried. Some have spent years trying to learn what happened to their relatives without ever being able to recover their remains.


Cemeteries in the mountains


The remains of many people who lost their lives in clashes are believed to be buried in areas stretching across Besta, Gabar, Herekol, Garzan, Cudi and Mava-Faraşin, particularly in the region encompassing Siirt, Batman (Êlih), Bitlis, Şırnak and Hakkari.


Some of these burial sites were established by relatives of those who lost their lives and by civilians living in the region. Figures of symbolic importance to the Kurdish movement, including Azime, Mehmet Goyi and Kendal, are also reported to be buried in these cemeteries.


The fate of thousands of people in Turkey remains unknown as a result of the intense conflict and unsolved killings of the 1990s. For years, the Saturday Mothers/People have continued their struggle for the missing to be found, the circumstances of their disappearance to be investigated and their fate to be disclosed.


Historical background of violations against the dead


Violations against the bodies of the dead have a long history in Turkey. From 1915 to Dersim, from Zilan to Newala Qesaba, and from the 1990s to the present day, practices such as withholding remains from families, keeping bodies in morgues for prolonged periods, obstructing burials, burying people without identification and destroying cemeteries have been documented at different times.


The IHD and families of the missing are calling for sites believed to contain mass graves to be protected and for evidence to be safeguarded against destruction through construction, roadworks or other forms of intervention.


For families, the fundamental demands are the definitive identification of missing persons, the return of their remains and recognition of their right to mourn.


The excavation of graves is not regarded as an ordinary digging operation, but as a process that must be carried out in accordance with forensic and archaeological standards. Families and human rights organisations are calling for evidence to be preserved, remains to be recovered using appropriate methods and identification procedures to be conducted according to scientific standards in line with the United Nations’ Minnesota Protocol.


Experts warn that uncontrolled excavations using heavy machinery such as excavators and bulldozers can damage biological and forensic evidence. For this reason, forensic specialists, anthropologists, archaeologists and other relevant experts should be involved in the excavation of mass graves.

title: CDK-S and YJK-S call for participation in 2nd Kurdish Culture and Arts Festival
content:
Final preparations are underway for the 2nd Kurdish Culture and Arts Festival, which will take place tomorrow, Saturday 29 August in Zurich, Switzerland.


The Festival Organizing Committee met at the Zurich Democratic Kurdish Community Center (Dem-Kurd) to review the final preparations. During the meeting, freedom guerrillas whose deaths were announced in recent days were also commemorated.


Following the meeting, the Democratic Kurdish Council of Switzerland (CDK-S) and the Kurdish Women’s Union of Switzerland (YJK-S) issued a joint statement calling for participation in the festival.


 


Speaking on behalf of the Festival Organizing Committee, artist Kawa Urmiye emphasized the significance of this year’s festival and said: “Although the announcement of these martyrdoms has caused deep sorrow among our people both in the homeland and in the diaspora, we will act in accordance with the wishes of our martyrs. We will uphold our values in line with their message: ‘Do not mourn endlessly for us or wear black because of us. If you are followers of our struggle, you must carry the banner of freedom even further.’


We call on our people to participate in the festival on August 29. By attending with all our colors and diversity, we must respond to the heroes of our homeland. We invite all our people to join us on Saturday at Zurich’s Hardturm Areal to commemorate all heroes, represented by Comrade Egîd, the immortal commander of the August 15 Initiative.”


Tribute to the martyrs of Kurdistan


The joint statement of CDK-S and YJK-S was read by CDK-S Co-Chair Dilan Çetinkaya. Paying tribute to the guerrillas whose deaths are currently being published, the statement said: “In this historic period we are living through, we experience both the joy and sorrow of moving toward peace with hope. For years, the brave sons and daughters of the Kurdish people waged an uncompromising struggle to reach this stage. For the free future of their people, they never let the torch of freedom fall from their hands. In recent times, the freedom movement has announced the martyrdom of many comrades who gave their lives without hesitation for freedom.


We remember these martyrs of freedom with respect and gratitude. We extend our condolences to their families and to the people of Kurdistan. We bow respectfully before their memory and once again renew our commitment and promise to keep their memory alive in our struggle.”


 


We will uphold the legacy of the martyrs


The statement emphasized that the festival would be held in the spirit of August 15 and called on people to uphold the legacy of the martyrs. The statement added: “On this basis, it is the responsibility of all of us to protect the legacy and values of our martyred comrades and to take our place in this historic process. Everyone must participate on the basis of Leader Apo’s philosophy and the paradigm of women’s freedom. Everyone must clearly fulfill their role.”


Festival dedicated to the martyrs


The CDK-S and YJK-S said that this year’s festival is dedicated to the martyrs and added: “For this reason, we are determined to hold our festival in the spirit of August 15. This year, we dedicate our traditional August 15 Initiative Festival to our martyrs whose martyrdoms were recently announced. We salute them with the spirit of the August 15 resistance. We aim to organize our festival in a manner worthy of the memory of our martyrs.


Dear people, we once again emphasize the importance of the festival we will hold during this historic period. Let us come together and rekindle the torch of freedom under the guidance of our martyrs at this festival. Let us share our grief together and organize our lives under the slogan ‘Free Leadership, Free Tomorrows.’


On this basis, as YJK-S and CDK-S, we call on our people living in Switzerland to support the festival, strengthen the struggle for freedom and peace, and contribute to the construction of a democratic future. We invite all our institutions and organizations to uphold the common values of our people and the legacy our martyrs have left us, and to join together in advancing the struggle to realize their dreams.”


The program of the festival


The 2nd Kurdish Culture and Arts Festival in Switzerland will be held this year at Hardturm Areal in Zurich under the slogan: “Building a democratic society with the spirit of the August 15 resistance.”


The festival will feature performances by Koma Agirê Jiyan, Tara Memedova …

title: Füsun Demirel: Let’s work together to build lasting peace
content:
Füsun Demirel said peace cannot be reduced to the silencing of guns and stressed the need to create spaces of freedom. Demirel said: “Koma Amed, a group whose music I deeply admire, should be able to tour the Black Sea region. Likewise, a Black Sea folk dance ensemble should be able to perform in Diyarbakır (Amed). There is so much to be done from this point onwards: joint projects, work by universities, bilingual collaborative productions... I will believe in genuine peace when Kurdish identity and the Kurdish language are truly recognised.” Demirel stressed that artists and academics should be involved in the process.


Actress and translator Füsun Demirel answered ANF’s questions about the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


Demirel stated art could serve as a powerful means of breaking down prejudice and said: “That is one of art’s fundamental purposes. One of its most powerful social functions is its ability to help people break down their prejudices. It enables people to think about the ‘other,’ to empathise, to see, feel and reach out to the ‘other.’ Through the medium it creates, art draws people into a story and, for a while, allows us to see the world through the eyes of that person, through the eyes of the ‘other.’ It enables us to identify with people and situations that are different from ourselves and towards which we may have held prejudices.


One of the examples I know best is the film Büyük Adam Küçük Aşk (Big Man, Little Love). The relationship between Rıfat Bey, a retired judge, and Hejar, a young Kurdish girl, is a very good example of this. The film tells an exemplary story for the peoples of Turkey. A country in which people like Rıfat Bey can change, where love, conscience and empathy prevail, is by no means an impossible dream. I am certain that people who once viewed life as Rıfat Bey does reconsidered their prejudices after watching the film.”


Turkish and Kurdish mothers should embrace one another


Füsun Demirel stressed, “As a Turkish mother, I can understand the pain of a Kurdish mother,” and continued: “If peace is to come, the first step should be for Turkish and Kurdish mothers who have suffered and lost their children to embrace one another. Unfortunately, we can also see that the prejudices within society and the polarising language being used could make this process more difficult. But whatever happens, we trust in the conscience, compassion and common sense of the people of this land.”


Demirel continued by describing the role art can play in breaking down prejudice. She said: “Another of the countless examples I have experienced was Aşk Dersleri (Lessons in Love), a play I performed in many years ago. The play focused particularly on issues affecting women, including violence against women, rape, menopause, first sexual experiences, menstruation and orgasm. As I told the story, I realised how much my own taboos challenged me. But I needed to talk about these issues openly to both women and men, to help people overcome their prejudices about women’s issues and sexuality, and to encourage men to empathise.


We really made considerable progress. The play ran for five years. Over the years, male audience members who came backstage told us that they had ‘assumed’ they were satisfying their partners, but after seeing the play they began to question that assumption and realised they needed to talk about these issues again with their partners. One prejudice after another was being broken down. I became convinced that we had created a difficult but necessary play. Art is one of the most powerful means we have of helping people dismantle their prejudices, one by one.”


Art creates space for reckoning and memory


Asked what the relationship between art and reckoning with the past could teach us in the current process, Demirel said: “Of course, it can teach us something very important about the current peace process: peace is not merely a political agreement. It is also a society’s capacity to hear one another’s stories, to hear the story of the ‘other.’ This is where art opens up an important space.


Reckoning is not simply about engaging with the ‘past.’ It brings to the surface the questions and stories of those who suffered, those who remained silent, those who objected, those who stood their ground, those who bowed and submitted, those whose stories were left unfinished, and those who never reached out to one another or were unable to do so. title: PAJK and KJK call on Kurds and their friends to keep the dreams of the martyrs alive
content:
The coordination bodies of the Party of Free Women of Kurdistan (PAJK) and the Kurdistan Women’s Community (KJK) commemorated those whose deaths were recently announced and extended their condolences to their families and the Kurdish people. In a joint statement, PAJK and KJK also commemorated members of the Kurdish freedom movement who lost their lives in August.


The women’s organizations stated that carrying forward the goals of the martyrs means participating in the building of a democratic society and intensifying the struggle for the physical freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan.


The statement, titled “To All Our Esteemed Families, Our Patriotic People and the Democratic Public,” reads as follows:


“The greatest value of the Kurdish people is the martyrs who fought for a free country and a dignified life and gave their lives for this cause. Throughout the course of our struggle, we have lost hundreds of esteemed comrades every month. On the occasion of August, we commemorate all those who fell during this month with love, respect and gratitude, in the persons of our comrades Jiyan (Yıldız Durmuş), Ekin Van, Deniz Fırat, Erdal, Kasım Engin, Atakan Mahir and Mustafa Yöndem.


They stood against injustice and the undignified life imposed upon the Kurdish people and turned toward the mountains of Kurdistan. We know that the true architects of all the gains we have achieved today are our self-sacrificing martyrs. As women and as a people, we have reached where we are today on the foundation of their legacy, and we will build our future upon it as well. We know that every endeavor founded upon the legacy of our incomparable martyrs will lead us to success.


Rêber Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] said, “Do not bury the martyrs in the earth, but in your hearts.” In doing so, he expressed how we should live with our martyrs. For every person who has found a place in our hearts is both a reason for us to struggle and a light that illuminates our path.


They fought for a free life and to forge a free Kurdish identity, leaving us a profound legacy. Through their lives, their struggle and their efforts to build a free life, they answered for us the question, “How should we live?” They were those who devoted themselves to a free life. Expecting nothing in return, they lived as some of the humblest and most beautiful people in this world, always giving of themselves.


They became the successors of Hayri Durmuş, who asked that the words, “He departed still indebted to his people,” be inscribed on his gravestone, and of Zîlan, who said, “If only we had something other than our lives that we could give.”


Dear patriotic people,


As you know, one of the decisions of the PKK’s 12th Congress was to announce the deaths of those whose deaths could not previously be made public due to the severe conditions of war. In this context, the deaths of numerous comrades are currently being announced in Amed, Istanbul, Van, Gever and Cizîra Botan, while commemorations are also being held for those whose deaths have already been announced.


We extend our condolences, in particular, to the families of our martyrs and to our entire people. We renew our pledge to our martyrs to build a free country and a dignified life. Our people commemorate their sons and daughters with great dignity and determination and pledge to remain faithful to their memory. The mass participation in funeral ceremonies and commemorative events is a response to the call of Rêber Apo and our martyrs. In particular, the stance, conviction and commitment of the mothers at these commemorations call upon us to devote ourselves even more resolutely to the struggle and bring it to success.


The heaviest price of our struggle spanning more than half a century has undoubtedly been the deaths of these esteemed comrades. The announcement of their deaths has created a deeply emotional atmosphere among our people and among us, while at the same time further strengthening our determination to struggle.


Our first promises were made to them. We promised to fulfill their hopes, dreams and aspirations. We said that nothing they had begun would be left unfinished. For we know that none of our comrades said, “We are dying, and everything is over.” On the contrary, through this struggle they recognized the life worth embracing.


As unparalleled defenders and builders of the struggle and the path of a free life, they opened the doors to a meaningful and free life for us women. When …

title: The pain and resistance hidden in the stones of Derase
content:
Some had been swept here by the wind like fallen leaves; others arrived clutching the last handfuls of hope left from a homeland consumed by flames. Undoubtedly, they were the children of the sun; they knew the secret of rising again from their own ashes. Though they had left behind immense tragedies, unrelenting pain, and rivers of tears, within the womb of hope they were always carrying the promise of a new dawn.


And so, they had not vanished. Those who reigned over the darkness had failed to erase these ancient names from the face of the earth. They were simply waiting—for that blessed day when the sun would rise never to set again; for the moment when Derwêş’s twelve cavalrymen would return, when they would reclaim the history buried in that land and crown it anew from the ashes of ruins and devastation.


Now we, too, stand on the threshold of this dawn, tracing the remnants of a hidden history on the rugged slopes of Shengal—a history left behind by different civilizations and buried beneath the soil of time.


In an age when the outside world ground humanity down through struggles for power, relentless massacres, and devastating famines, there were ancient valleys sheltered behind immense mountains. For centuries, this land became the one gateway to salvation for countless peoples who had lost their homelands, despite their different languages and beliefs. While these majestic mountains, with their rocky chests, bore the merciless storms raging beyond them, their fertile soil nurtured every wounded soul who sought refuge there with the same compassion.


Under the dark shadow of genocide and massacres, the Yazidi and Armenian peoples, bound by a shared fate, were no strangers to one another’s wounds. In 1915, when Armenians were subjected to the Ottoman Empire’s brutal policies of deportation and extermination, they found one of the safest places of refuge in Yazidi lands. It was an unshakable bond of trust forged through a shared memory of suffering.


When we sift through the ashes of the past, what emerges is an epic of resistance by two ancient peoples struggling to survive amid the rugged geography of the Middle East. In the aftermath of 1915, one group of Armenians made their way toward the mountains of Shengal.


Derase was one of the foremost sacred refuges where those seeking shelter on the rugged slopes of Shengal and in the homeland of the Yazidis made their home. Today, every step we take in Derase, every stone that catches our eye, is laden with the profound sorrow of that era. The atmosphere carries us beyond the boundaries of time, making us relive the past through the pain of the present. All that remained from those days were ruins and stone chambers—

shikefts

—where memories had taken refuge. Each shikeft bore the hidden seal of immense tragedy and an unyielding will to survive.


This river of suffering would flow once again along the same course in 2014, with one of the gravest genocidal campaigns of the 21st century. Faced with a dark campaign that sought to uproot Yazidism and erase it from the face of the earth, the Yazidi people, guided by their historical memory, once again sought refuge in Derase. At that terrifying moment, when the world turned its back and fled and darkness descended upon Shengal like a nightmare, freedom fighters carrying the banner of human dignity advanced against the darkness and changed the course of history.


It was no coincidence that the twelve cavalrymen who came to confront the latest Yazidi Genocide turned this place into a stronghold of resistance; this place carried the echoes of an ancient tradition. What was being targeted in the persons of the twelve cavalrymen who resisted there, were the Armenian roots whose memory was sought to be erased and the unyielding resistance of the Yazidis.


For the first time, through these twelve cavalrymen, history reversed a tragic fate woven with suffering. Derase was no longer merely a refuge for survival; it became a monument to resistance, crowned with the victory of Yazidi heroism and dignity.


As our footsteps echo across the stones of this ancient land, its haunting atmosphere envelops our souls. Every trace of the past seems to gaze back at the present through the mirror of history. And the valley’s timeless wind whispers the same lullaby to every weary soul who crosses its threshold:


“Rest. You are safe here; this is the shared home of wounded humanity.”

title: Iranian forces arrest five Kurdish men in Ilam province
content:
Iranian forces have arrested Kurdish citizens Milad Alaei-Nasab, Amin Nasseri, Yasser Havasizadeh, Rouhollah Gholami and Younes Bekri without warrants in Darreh Shahr, Asemanabad and Sarableh, Ilam Province, over the past week.


The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that on 23 August, officers of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organisation shot Nasseri in the leg and arrested him after he was wounded.


Nasseri, a Kurdish singer from Asemanabad, had been wanted by the security agencies following the December 2025–January 2026 protests.


Security forces arrested Gholami and Bekri, two other citizens from Asemanabad, at the same time.


On 24 August, security forces surrounded the Pir Hamzeh area of Asemanabad and violently arrested Havasizadeh.


Three days later, on 27 August, security forces arrested Alaei-Nasab, from Darreh Shahr, in the city.


Despite the families’ attempts to obtain information about the five, the security and judicial authorities have refused to respond or provide any explanation about their situation.


No information is available regarding the reasons for the arrests or the charges brought against them.

title: PYD: Syria’s new constitution must recognize the Kurdish people, their rights and language
content:
The Democratic Union Party (PYD) issued a written statement regarding the latest developments in Syria. The party described some of the steps taken recently in Syria as positive and important, while stressing that these developments are not sufficient to provide a comprehensive solution to the Kurdish question.


The PYD particularly welcomed the steps toward integrating the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into state institutions, as well as the developments concerning the Kurdish language, which will be permitted to be taught in public and private schools in areas where Kurds constitute a significant portion of the population.


The statement noted that these developments are important for the construction of a new Syria, saying: “These developments are positive and important steps, but they are not sufficient. The Kurdish question in Syria is a fundamental issue, and the rights of the Kurdish people must be an integral part of the constitutional and political framework of the new Syria.”


The statement stressed that Kurdish participation in building state institutions and in the country’s political, military, administrative and cultural life represents a source of strength for Syria, emphasizing that such participation would reinforce the country’s unity and stability.


The PYD also stated that the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) should be integrated into the state’s official institutions.


The integration of the YPJ, it added, should be carried out in a manner that reflects the role and status of women in building the new Syria.


The PYD also outlined its demands regarding Syria’s new constitution, stating that the Kurdish people should receive constitutional recognition.


The statement said: “Syria’s new constitution must explicitly recognize the Kurdish people as a united and constituent people in Syria; it must recognize the Kurdish language and the political, cultural and national rights of the Kurdish people. In doing so, it must establish the principle of genuine partnership among all components of Syrian society.”


The PYD pointed out that the new Syria should be built on the principles of democracy, partnership and recognition of diversity, calling for the rights of all peoples and communities to be constitutionally guaranteed.


In conclusion, the statement stressed that the steps taken in Syria are welcomed but need to be complemented by new constitutional arrangements, describing this as “the path toward genuine partnership and a strong Syria enriched by its diversity and by all its peoples and communities.”

author: The Canadian Press
title: Greenland reports were split on whether forced contraception of Indigenous women, girls constituted genocide
content:
Two reports investigating the forcible contraception of thousands of Indigenous women and girls in Greenland by Danish health authorities for decades were split over whether the practice

constituted genocide.


The Greenlandic government, which commissioned the inquiry, released the reports Friday but, when pressed by journalists during a news conference, would not say whether its leaders concluded whether a genocide had occurred.


The government told the authors to use the definition under the United Nations’ 1948 genocide convention, which includes “imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group.”


Known as the “spiral case,

 ” the revelations rocked both Denmark and Greenland. More than 350 Greenlandic Indigenous women and girls, including some 12 years old and younger, previously came forward to investigators and reported that they were

forcibly given contraception by Danish health authorities

. Denmark says more than 4,000 women and girls — reportedly half the fertile women in Greenland at the time — received IUDs between the 1960s and mid-1970s.


The Inuit victims, many of them teenagers at the time, said they were either fitted with intrauterine contraceptive devices, known as IUDs or coils, or given a hormonal birth control injection. They were not told details about the procedure, or did not give their consent.


The alleged purpose was to limit population growth in Greenland by preventing pregnancies. The population on the Arctic island was rapidly increasing at the time because of better living conditions and better health care.


The cases occurred between the 1960s and the early 1990s. Greenland took over its own healthcare programs on Jan. 1, 1992.


The Danish government on Thursday approved payouts of 

300,000 Danish kroner

 (about $46,500) to each victim. 

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen

 officially apologized last year.


Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a reconciliation commission would be set up, a move that Frederiksen endorsed in a statement Friday.


Authors split findings into two reports


Also on Friday, the Greenlandic government only accepted the findings of one of the reports, saying that an expert found that the second — the one that definitively said a genocide had not taken place — did not meet recognized scientific standards.


The reports come as 

U.S. President Donald Trump pushes to control

 the Arctic island, which is a self-governing territory of Denmark. The leaders of Greenland and Denmark say the island is not for sale and 

only Greenlanders can decide their fate.


“There is no empirical evidence to assume that any Danish or Greenlandic authority, or any individual healthcare professional, at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population or a significant proportion of it,” the authors of the rejected report wrote. “There was no genocide.”


The accepted report, however, did not conclude whether there was a genocide. The authors wrote that they were not able to determine if any intent to destroy the population existed solely through the forcible contraception cases, and suggested further study that encompassed other Danish practices at the time that affected Greenlandic children and families. The authors did not, unlike the other report, conclusively say a genocide did not occur.


“It is difficult to imagine circumstances in which an attempt to substantially reduce the population of a single ethnic group could not constitute an intent to destroy, in part, that ethnicity,” the report said.


The reports were originally supposed to be a single publication but two of the four members of the group broke away several months ago and wrote their own report. Theirs was the one rejected by the island’s government; one of the authors is a former director of the Danish Institute for Human Rights.


“The reason given was professional disagreements amongst the members and, to some extent, concerns about the geopolitical situation,” the Greenlandic government said Friday in a news release.


The news release did not elaborate on what the two authors considered to be the geopolitical situation.


Read more:


Denmark and Greenland apologize for painful legacy of forced Inuit contraception

Greenland reports were split on whether forced contraception of Indigenous women, girls constituted genocide

author: DebConf 25
title: Reviving (un)schroot?
content:
by Helmut Grohne


At: DebConf25


https://debconf25.debconf.org/talks/170-reviving-unschroot/


The schroot tool has been the primary build backend used by sbuild for a long time. More and more work has gone into a new unshare backend that we are slowly transitioning to. It solves several problems with schroot ranging from convenience, via security to reproducibility. However, the unshare backend comes with several downsides. Effectively, it bundles a container runtime into sbuild. The new backend inevitably regresses some use cases such as conveniently interacting with chroot environments outside builds. The question arises: Can we provide the improvements gained from unshare via the schroot API to sbuild? I will present a proof-of-concept, its limitations and request feedback regarding what features are needed to make it practically useful.


Room: Grand amphi

title: ᖃᓄᖅ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥᐅᑕᑦ ᐱᕚᓪᓕᕈᑎᖃᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ

From whales to drones, how northerns could benefit from increased defence spending in North

.


ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᖏᒡᓕᒋᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᕗᖅ ᑐᑭᓕᐊᖓᓂ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᑭᐅᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᓚᖕᓄᑦ-ᐱᓕᐊᓐ ᑖᓚᓂ ᐅᐊᖕᓇᒥ ᐊᑦᓛᓐᑎᒃᒥ ᐊᖏᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᒥ ᐊᖏᖅᓯᒪᓂᖓᓐᓂ, ᐅᖃᖅᐳᖅ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖅ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ.


ᔭᓄᕈᓪ ᔭᓂ ᑭᐊᕆᒡᓇᓐ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐋᒍᔅᑎ 19−ᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥ ᓯᕗᓕᐅᖅᑎᐅᔪᓂ, ᐊᒻᒪᓗᑦᑕᐅᖅ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᙳᐊᓂ, ᐅᖃᓪᓚᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᔪᓯᔪᒥ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᖓᓂ ᖁᕝᕙᕆᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂᑦ.


ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖃᖃᑕᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓃᓯᒪᕗᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᕿᑎᐊᓃᖦᖢᓂ ᑕᐃᒪᙵᓂ ᒫᒃ ᑳᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕐᔪᐊᙳᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᒫᔾᔨ 2025−ᒥ. ᓕᐳᕈᒃᑯᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᖓᑦ ᒧᓕᓂᕋᐃᓯᒪᕗᖅ ᑭᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ ᐅᐊᖕᓇᒥ ᐊᑦᓛᓐᑎᒃᒥ ᐊᖏᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᒥ, ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ NATO, ᐊᖏᒡᓕᒋᐊᖅᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᖏᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑐᓂᓯᕙᖕᓂᖓᓂ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᖏᓐᓂ 5 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓂᑯᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓄᑦ ᑲᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ 2035−ᖑᕋᓱᖕᓂᖓᓂ.


ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑭᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ 2 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᓱᓕᓂᕋᕈᒻᒥ — ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ $81.1 ᐱᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓂᑯᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓄᑦ ᑲᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ — ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ 2025−ᒥ.


ᑭᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐆᒥᖓ ᐊᖏᖅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑳᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒧᑦ ᑕᑯᒋᐊᖅᓯᒪᕗᖅ, ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓪᓗᓂ ᐅᓄᕐᓂᖅᓴᐅᔪᓂ $40 ᐱᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᓄᑖᙳᕆᐊᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖓᕙᕆᐊᖅᓯᒪᔪᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕈᑎᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᕿᓚᖏᒥ ᖄᖅᑕᔫᓂ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᕈᑕᐅᔪᓂ.


ᐅᓇ ᓄᑖᖑᔪᖅ ᑕᑯᔭᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᕗᖅ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ, ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᓄᓇᓕᐅᔪᓂ, ᐊᔭᐅᕆᓂᕐᒥ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᖏᒡᓕᒋᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᓂ ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᓲᕐᓗ ᐱᙳᐊᕐᕕᓂᑦ, ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᕕᖕᓂ.


ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᑦ ᑭᐅᓗᒃᐳᑦ ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᓚᖕᓄᑦ−ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᖃᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ, ᑐᑭᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐊᑑᑎᖃᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᑐᐃᓐᓇᕐᓄᑦ.


ᑭᐊᕆᒡᓇᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓱᒫᓂᒃᐳᑦ ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇᒐᓚᒃ.


“ᐱᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᐊᖅᐳᒍᑦ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᓂ ᐆᒪᙵᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᒡᕕᐊᕈᒪᙱᓚᒍᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓄᑦ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑭᐊᕆᒡᓇᓐ, ᑎᒃᑯᐊᕆᓪᓗᓂ ᐱᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᖏᒡᓕᒋᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐆᒻᒪᖅᑯᑎᓂ, ᑯᕕᖅᑕᖅᑕᐅᓂᕐᒥ, ᐃᒪᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑭᐊᖅᑭᕕᒃᑰᕈᓐᓇᐅᑎᓂ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᑕᖃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ.


ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᓚᐅᕆᕗᖅ ᖁᓕᒥᒎᓕᕋᓛᓂ, ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᐃᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᙳᐊᓂ, ᐊᒃᓱᕈᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᒫᓐᓇᒨᓕᖓᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖃᐅᑎᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ.


“ᖃᐅᔨᔭᕆᐊᖃᖅᐳᒍᑦ ᕿᓚᓗᒐᕐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ,ᓗᑦᑕᐅᖅ ᐃᒪᐅᑉ ᐊᑖᓃᓲᓂ ᐅᒥᐊᕐᓂ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ, “ᑕᐃᒫᒃ ᖁᓕᒥᒎᓕᕋᓛᑦ ᐊᓯᐊᖑᓗᓂ ᐆᒃᑑᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᐳᖅ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᓚᖕᓄᑦ-ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᑎᓂ.”


ᑲᑎᒪᖃᑎᖃᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑭᐊᕆᒡᓇᓐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᓐᓂ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᔨᕐᔪᐊᖑᔪᓂ ᐋᒍᔅᑎ 19−ᒥ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ, ᓯᕗᓕᖅᑎ ᔮᓐ ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᕆᐊᓪᓚᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᓯᒪᔭᖓᓂ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᕆᓚᐅᖅᓯᒪᔭᖓᓂ ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐊᖏᒡᓕᒋᐊᖅᑐᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ.


“ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓪᓗᐊᕆᕗᖅ ᐊᑯᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᕚᓪᓕᕈᑎᓂ ᓄᓇᕘᑉ ᓄᓇᓕᖏᓐᓄᑦ, ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᕙᐃᔅᐳᒃᑯᑦ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ.


ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒥ ᓇᓚᐅᑦᑖᕆᓂᖃᙱᓚᖅ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐃᓚᑰᓂᐅᔪᒥ, ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑕᐱᕇᑦ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᓂᐊᖑᔪᒥ 2020−ᒥ ᓇᓚᐅᑦᑖᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᒥ $75.1 ᐱᓕᐊᓐ−ᖑᓂᖓᓂ.


ᐱᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖃᖅᐳᖅ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓄᓇᓕᐅᔪᓂ, ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐸᖕᒥᐅᓗᐊᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᓂᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᖓᓂᐅᔪᓂ, ᓄᑕᐅᔪᓐᓃᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᔪᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᓂᑦ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᖃᖅᑐᓂ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᒪᕐᒥ ᓴᓗᒻᒪᖅᓴᐃᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᓂ ᓄᖑᓪᓕᓂᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᓕᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓪᓗᑎᒃ.


ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᒃᐳᑦ ᐊᕕᒃᓯᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᑎᑭᓛᖅᑐᒥ 5 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ ᐅᐊᖕᓇᒥ ᐊᑦᓛᓐᑎᒃᒥ ᐊᖏᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᒥ ᑐᓂᓯᓗᑎᒃ 3.5 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᑐᕌᖓᔪᒧᑦ ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ 1.5 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᓚᖕᓄᑦ-ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ. ᐅᓇ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᓇᔭᖅᐳᖅ $60 ᐱᓕᐊᓐᓄᑦ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᓚᖕᓄᑦ-ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᐅᔪᓄᑦ 2035−ᒥ, ᐅᓇᑕᖅᑐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᓇᓚᐅᑦᑖᕆᕗᑦ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᒥ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᕕᕗᐊᕆᒥ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᖅᑎᖏᑦᑕ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔪᒃᓴᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᔨᐅᔪᒧᑦ.


ᑭᒃᑯᓕᒫᑦ ᐊᖏᖃᑎᖃᙱᓚᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ, ᑳᔭ ᑐᐳᐃ, ᐊᑦᑎᖕᓂᖅᓴᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᐊᖕᓇᒥ ᐊᑦᓛᓐᑎᒃᒥ ᐊᖏᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᒥ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ, ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᒡᔪᐊᒥ ᑐᕌᓐᑐᒥ−ᑐᙵᕕᓕᖕᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᑎᙵᓂᐅᔪᒥ, ᐊᐱᕆᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᔫᓂ 17−ᒥ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᓇ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᓚᖕᓄᑦ-ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑕᐅᑐᒃᑕᑐᐊᖃᑲᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑕᑯᔭᐅᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᖓᓂ “ᐃᓱᒪᑐᓂᕐᒥ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᒥ.”


“ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᒍᓂ ᖃᔅᓯᒐᒪᖕᓄᑦ-ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᒥᒃ ᑲᑎᙵᑎᑦᑎᔪᒥ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥ 5 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒧᑦ ᑐᕌᒐᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᑦ, ᐱᔪᒪᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᔭᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᐳᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᓂ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᕐᔪᐊᖑᔪᓂ ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᓇᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ ᐸᕐᓇᒍᑕᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᖏᖅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᒥ,” ᑐᐳᐃ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᒥ.


ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ, ᑭᐊᕆᒡᓇᓐ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᙱᓚᖅ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᕆᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᖃᖓ ᐱᔭᕇᖅᓯᒪᓂᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᓄᑖᖑᔪᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᓖᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᐸᒃᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᔪᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᐅᔪᓄᑦ. ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᔨᕐᔪᐊᖑᔪᓂ ᐅᖃᖃᑎᖃᖅᐳᑦ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᑭᓱᓂ ᐱᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ.


“ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ ᐃᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓃᓐᓂᖅᓴᐅᕗᑦ ᐊᓯᖏᓐᓂ; ᑐᓴᐅᒪᔾᔪᑎᒃᓴᖃᕐᓂᖅᓴᐅᕗᒍᑦ, ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐱᕕᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐅᖃᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᕗᖅ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.

author: DebConf 25
title: Guidelines for Boosting Long-Lasting FLOSS Contributors
content:
by David Tadokoro


At: DebConf25


https://debconf25.debconf.org/talks/160-guidelines-for-boosting-long-lasting-floss-contributors/


Free Libre and Open Source Software (FLOSS) development is a validated approach to producing cutting-edge software solutions used by governments, companies, and society at large. At the core of all FLOSS software projects are communities composed primarily of developers who evolve and maintain the software while devising rules for the development process. A common problem is the renewal and/or scaling of the workforce, which is not about encouraging waves of new and sporadic contributors but about fostering long-lasting ones that can have a more profound impact on the project. This work presents guidelines for mentoring students to build skills and gain experience essential to becoming valuable assets in most FLOSS ecosystems. Beyond a reasonable software development background, previous experience in FLOSS development is not a requirement. These guidelines are a product of a 15-weeks university course where students had to (1) learn the fundamentals of Linux kernel development and send patches to a subsystem, (2) contribute to supporting tools to the GNU/Linux ecosystem, (3) introduce software packaging in the context of Debian, and finally (4) contribute to a chosen FLOSS project. The method reproduces the natural way a "self-taught" contributor would enter a FLOSS ecosystem (heavily inspired by how Debian does it), though in a more focused and immersive environment. Through in-loco workshops, accessible and knowledgeable mentors, and close and constant monitoring, we simulated a smaller FLOSS community where students (inexperienced contributors) learned from mentors (maintainers); we argue that this simulated community can be more efficient than a real one as feedback is faster and more adapted to each contributor, and concepts can be abstracted and simplified for easier absorption. Our results show that the method fostered (1) developers who are more confident in contributing to any FLOSS project and beyond to the "one-commit contributor"  and (2) the enhancement of fundamental hard skills (like Git and Web/email-based contribution models) and soft skills (like communication and feedback assimilation) for any FLOSS project. Even though deep technical knowledge becomes mandatory for every contributor in a specific project, we claim that implementing the proposed guidelines can quickly nurture tens of developers with a solid base for becoming long-lasting contributors to FLOSS.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Democrat Calls for Criminal Probe of RFK Jr. for Lying in Confirmation Hearing
content:
“RFK’s platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake,” said Sen. Ron Wyden.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) has called for a criminal investigation into Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., after the strongest evidence yet of Kennedy lying about his anti-vaccine campaigning during his Senate confirmation hearings has emerged — amid a fresh measles crisis spurred by his policies.

“RFK’s platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake. There are consequences for lying to Congress,” said Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. It’s unlikely that the Trump administration would prosecute their own secretary, but Wyden said that he is pressuring Republicans to refer Kennedy to the Department of Justice for an investigation.

“And when Democrats retake the majority in the Senate, RFK will be at the top of the list of Trump officials the finance committee will hold accountable for endangering American families,” continued Wyden, who grilled Kennedy on his trip to Samoa during his confirmation hearings last year.

Kennedy repeatedly told senators that his visit to Samoa in June 2019 “had nothing to do with vaccines,” instead saying that he went to “introduce a medical informatics system that would digitize records.” But records show the trip was organized for him to advocate against the MMR vaccine, fueling an anti-vaccine movement in the country. In a measles outbreak just a few months after his visit 83 people died, most of them children.

In past months, email evidence from a U.S. embassy official in Samoa found that RFK Jr. lied, with the official saying that the “real reason” for his visit was to raise “health concerns associated with vaccinating (from his point of view).”

On Thursday, new reports revealed documents in which Kennedy personally detailed the purpose of the trip, contradicting his testimony.

“I am writing this letter to you in the hope that we might be helpful to the people of your great nation,” Kennedy wrote to Samoa’s prime minister. The letter is dated January 20, 2019, and is written on the letterhead of his anti-vaccine group, Children’s Health Defense.

He cited his debunked claim that the MMR vaccine causes adverse health effects, repeating a conspiracy theory that the vaccine caused two deaths in the country which were actually attributed to a nurse errantly mixing the vaccine with expired muscle relaxant.

“I would propose my team conduct detailed health informatics assessment in Samoa of what happened with your MMR vaccines,” Kennedy said.

Samoa’s then-prime minister, Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi, responded a month later welcoming Kennedy for an “independent health assessment of our MMR Vaccines.”

Samoan health officials said that his visit supercharged the anti-vaccine movement in the small island country, lending credibility to and amplifying anti-vaccine activists.

The new revelations, as well as his dismissal of two new measles-related deaths in the U.S. this week, have once again spurred calls for Kennedy to be removed.

“This is a pattern, not a slip. RFK Jr. has lied to the Senate, lied to the American people, and jeopardized the health of children to advance his anti-vaccine agenda,” said Sen. Ed Markey (Massachusetts), the top Democrat on the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee on Primary Health and Retirement Security. “He should never have been confirmed, and he cannot be trusted to run HHS for even one more day.”

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Admin Eyes Deal to Give Away Yosemite Park Land to Real Estate Firm
content:
The White House has been in talks with the firm since the spring of last year.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

For the past year, the National Park Service (NPS) has been in talks with a private corporation to negotiate a possible land deal, providing the company with a stretch of land located within Yosemite National Park.

The proposed deal, first reported by NOTUS, would benefit Kingsbarn Realty Capital, a real estate investment company, which owns 83 acres of land adjacent to the park. According to sources with knowledge of the proposal, Kingsbarn would be given the land to allow it to develop a road from its property to one of the more popular destinations in the park, a large grove of ancient sequoia trees just five miles away, to which the property doesn’t currently have easy road access.

Per the report, the Trump administration “has been looking into ways it could cede a roughly quarter-mile strip of land inside Yosemite.” The proposal also has the “full weight” of the Interior Department’s backing, which is causing friction with park staff.

“The political pressure being brought to bear is very unusual,” one source told NOTUS.

The proposal has been in the works since the spring of 2025. Notably, Interior Department Secretary Doug Burgum promised lawmakers during his confirmation hearings in January of that year that he would keep national parks intact.

“We need to support and protect every single inch of” U.S. national parks, he said at the time.

Federal rules require that land owned by the government and given to private companies must be done through exchanges of land elsewhere, and Kingsbarn would likely give away some of its land in California to the feds. But such a move has never occurred for land within a national park — indeed, national parks tend to grow in size rather than lose ground.

Even if the deal were a pure land swap, Kingsbarn could receive huge financial windfalls from it if the company built homes or hotels on its property near the park and proposed roadway.

“Obviously this looks kind of unseemly, with the value of this property potentially exploding with the deal,” a source familiar with the proposed exchange said. “It kind of smells, you know. It’s not quite right.”

Cicely Muldoon, the former superintendent of Yosemite National Park who resigned from her position just before Trump began his second term as president in 2025, panned the idea of giving away parts of Yosemite to the real estate company.

“The national park idea started in Yosemite with Abraham Lincoln’s preservation of Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias. Our basic purpose in the national parks is to preserve these places unimpaired for future generations, not letting go of that for the purpose of private profit,” Muldoon told NOTUS.

author: DebConf 25
title: Integrating Knowledge Graphs into the Debian Ecosystem
content:
by Alexander Belikov


At: DebConf25


https://debconf25.debconf.org/talks/99-integrating-knowledge-graphs-into-the-debian-ecosystem/


In an era where software systems are increasingly complex and interconnected, understanding and managing the relationships between packages, maintainers, dependencies, and vulnerabilities is paramount. This talk explores the innovative integration of knowledge graphs into the Debian ecosystem, offering a structured and semantic approach to package management and analysis.


We'll delve into how knowledge graphs can unify diverse data sources — such as package metadata, security advisories, and reproducibility reports — into an interconnected model that enhances visibility and reasoning capabilities. By representing entities (like packages and maintainers) and their relationships, we can facilitate advanced queries and insights that traditional systems may not easily provide.


Key Takeaways:


Semantic Integration: Learn how to map Debian's rich metadata into a coherent knowledge graph, enabling seamless integration and interoperability.

Enhanced Use Cases:

- Tracking and validating package dependencies.
- Identifying and analyzing vulnerability propagation.
- Assessing license compatibility and compliance.
- Auditing build reproducibility across packages.
- Highlighting Areas Lacking Reproducible Builds.
- Mapping Community Needs: Linking data from platforms like "grow-your-ideas" with package metadata to identify areas lacking attention
- Informing Funding Decisions: Providing data-driven insights to allocate resources effectively, ensuring that critical community needs are addressed.


Community Collaboration:


Understand how this approach can foster collaboration within the Debian community, providing tools for maintainers, developers, and researchers to contribute and benefit from shared insights.


Room: Petit amphi

author: DebConf 25
title: Using Debusine to pre-test your unstable uploads
content:
by Colin Watson


At: DebConf25


https://debconf25.debconf.org/talks/29-using-debusine-to-pre-test-your-unstable-uploads/


Debusine can build and run tests against your Debian uploads before sending them to the Debian archive. It can build your upload on multiple architectures and run the autopkgtests of your reverse dependencies against these builds. Only once everything has passed will your upload continue to Debian.


You can use this to pre-test your uploads to unstable, giving you confidence that your uploads will be able to migrate to testing. This is very useful during the freeze.


This talk is aimed at a broad audience of Debian contributors. We'll tell you what debusine is, if you haven't heard about it. For those who have, we’ll show you some of the features we’ve implemented in the last year, and how you can use them to do QA work in Debian right now. Including dput-ng integration, and scaling into clouds.


Debusine is a general-purpose software factory tailored to the needs of a Debian-based distribution. It manages the scheduling and distribution of tasks to distributed worker machines. It’s free software, implemented in Python, and packaged in the Debian archive.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Dilley ICE Jail Is “Commodification of Child Imprisonment,” says Joaquin Castro
content:
Calls to shut down the facility grow following the detention and deportation of a 5-year-old and his father.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Calls to shut down the ICE jail known as the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in South Texas continue to grow following the detention and deportation of 5-year-old Liam Tadeo and his father Victor Martinez Nieto to Mexico. According to the family’s lawyer, Nieto had begged officers to let his son go as they were arrested on their way to soccer practice in Austin last week. Nieto wanted Liam released to his mother, but ICE reportedly refused. The arrest happened just days before Liam was set to start kindergarten.

Texas Democratic Congressmember Joaquin Castro previously attempted to visit Liam and his father at Dilley but was denied by ICE. Last month, Castro led a group of more than 110 Democratic House members in a nationwide call to end family detention and shut down Dilley. “You have kids as young as 2 months old who have been in prison there,” says Castro. “And every child that’s put in there — every woman, every person — there are American investors who are making money off of their imprisonment.”

Castro notes that children are not supposed to be held in detention centers for more than 20 days. “I’ve met with kids who have been there three months, seven months, 10 months. And so, this is really abusive, and it’s traumatizing a lot of kids.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: In a moment, we’re going to be going to Nepal to talk about the massive devastation from a glacier that broke off. Now at least 2,000 people are dead or missing. But first, we go to Texas.

Calls to shut down the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in South Texas continue to grow following the detention and deportation of Victor Martinez Nieto, along with his 5-year-old son Liam. The arrest happened just days before Liam was set to start kindergarten. They’ve both been deported to Mexico. According to the family’s lawyer, Liam’s dad begged officers to let his son go as they were arrested on their way to soccer practice in Austin last week. His father wanted Liam to be released to his mom, but ICE reportedly refused.

We go now to San Antonio, Texas, where we’re joined by Democratic Congressmember Joaquin Castro, who requested to visit Liam and his father in custody, but ICE denied the request. Last month, Congressmember Castro led a group of more than 110 Democratic House members in a nationwide call to end the immigration jail in Dilley. He’s joining us now from a car in San Antonio on his way to a meeting.

Congressmember Castro, we thank you for taking these minutes to be with us. Talk about what you’re demanding. Today, you’re headed to Dilley once again.

REP. JOAQUIN CASTRO: Yeah, great to be with y’all.

This will be my ninth inspection of Dilley this year. And I join 110 other Democrats in calling for the United States government to shut down the Dilley detention center. It is — to me, it represents the commodification of child imprisonment. You have kids as young as 2 months old who have been in prison there. And every child that’s put in there — every woman, every person — there are American investors who are making money off of their imprisonment, but most especially the children. So, I got asked by some of ICE leadership to meet with them at Dilley, and I’m going to go do that this morning.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Congressman, The Texas Tribune reported earlier this month that immigrant children are held in Dilley five times longer than a court order allows. Can you talk about that situation, especially the case of Liam Tadeo, the 5-year-old boy, and his father, Victor Martinez Nieto?

REP. JOAQUIN CASTRO: Yeah, I tried to visit with Liam and his father last Friday and got his mother’s permission to meet with him, and still, ICE refused to let me meet with him. I then told them that I wanted to visit with Liam and his father today during my inspection, and they, of course, deported him in the last few days. And so, this is an agency that has become very abusive, that has absolutely gone rogue and that should be disbanded.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Congressman, could you comment also about how a a judge has blocked Minnesota’s bid to extradite Christian Castro, an ICE agent accused of firing his gun and wounding a Venezuelan man in …

author: Rizomatica
title: Carabineros implicados en el asesinato de Gabriel Sanhueza, El Vejetal, serán formalizados por homicidio y obstrucción a la justicia
content:
Según el Fiscal César Schibar, el día de ayer 27 de agosto, se materializó la detención de dos funcionarios de carabineros: Sebastián Zárate Palma y Manuel Méndez Muñoz; por su responsabilidad en el delito de homicidio y obstrucción a la investigación, por los hechos ocurridos el día 17 de agosto en horas de la madrugada, en el sector de Maquehue y que afectó a una de las víctimas, Gabriel Utreras Sanhueza, El Vejetal, quien resultó fallecido por el disparo de uno de los funcionarios policiales.


Básicamente se trató de un control de carabineros que estaba realizando en el ámbito de sus funciones y preliminarmente y conforme a la información entregada por dichos funcionarios, había existido un supuesto ataque de las víctimas, en este caso las personas civiles en contra de ellos, por lo cual utilizaron sus armas de fuego. Y aplicando la presunción de la ley de Nain Retamal, entonces se le dio el tratamiento preliminarmente de víctimas y testigos.


La investigación continuó y se lograron recabar una serie de antecedentes que permitieron desvirtuar esta presunción, toda vez que NO existió un uso racional de la fuerza y tampoco se pudo establecer que existiera una agresión por parte de las víctimas civiles.


Respecto de la dinámica de los hechos, se han recabado distintos elementos, y uno de ellos específicamente es un video, el cual será aportado al momento de la audiencia y el control de la detención. En este elemento se puede observar la AUSENCIA DE UN ATAQUE POR PARTE DE LAS VÍCTIMAS hacia carabineros y sí la reacción, sí la utilización, al menos de uno de los funcionarios de su arma de fuego disparando a corta distancia en contra del vehículo en que se transportaban las víctimas.


Ambos carabineros serán formalizados por el delito de homicidio en contra de las víctimas civiles que se transportaban en el interior del vehículo y además obstrucción a la investigación, pues ENTREGARON DATOS FALSOS, que fueron contrastados con elementos objetivos de manera imparcial, pudiendo establecerse que la versión que dieron no era fidedigna, lo que motivó entonces a la Fiscalía a solicitar la orden de detención respectiva.


Los funcionarios entregaron una versión inicial que los amparaba en la presunción que está establecida en la ley Nain Retamal que establece que debe dárseles un tratamiento de víctima o testigo a los funcionarios policiales que participan en un procedimiento, sin embargo, con la reunión de otros elementos se permitió desvirtuar la misma.


Este falso testimonio sobre el ataque y atropello de las víctimas hacia carabineros fue rápidamente difundido en la prensa, incluso por el fiscal Espinosa, quien estableció a priori que los funcionarios habían actuado en defensa propia, versión que ya se estimó como falsa.


La comunidad y familia de Gabriel, El Vejetal, han declarado que harán todo lo posible por establecer qué pasó y cuales fueron las responsabilidades, y piden se investiguen los antecedentes y que la justicia actúe con independencia y se conozca la verdad.
